Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 15, verse 1–5:

(p-269) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Hijr

This surah is Meccan.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieve will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will soon know.﴾ ﴿We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree.﴾ ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can it delay it.﴾

"Alif, Lam, Ra": the discussion of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of the surahs has already preceded. "Tilka" (these) may refer, according to some opinions, to the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-mu'jam). It is also possible that it refers to the wisdoms, lessons and the like that the verses of the Torah and the Gospel contained, and the Qur'an is conjoined to it. Mujahid and Qatada said: "the Book" in the verse is what was revealed of the books before the Qur'an. It is also possible that "the Book" is meant to be the Qur'an, and then the attribute is conjoined to it.

Nafi' and 'Asim read "rubama" with a light ba' (ب), and the rest read it with a shadda, except that Abu 'Amr read it both ways; both are dialects. It is related from Talha ibn Musarrif "rubbatama" with the addition of a ta', (p-270) and this is a dialect. "Rubama" is for paucity, though it may occasionally come for abundance. Some people said that this is from that, and from it is the line:

"Rubba ka'sin harraqta ya ibna Lu'ayy" (How many a cup you spilled, O son of Lu'ayy).

Al-Zajjaj denied that "rubba" comes for abundance.

The "ma" that "rubba" enters upon may be a indefinite noun in the sense of "shay'" (thing), and that is when there is in the speech a pronoun returning to it, like the saying of the poet:

"Rubbama takrahu al-nufusu mina al-amr lahu furjatun ka-hallil-iqal" (Perhaps the souls dislike a matter, for it there is a relief like the untying of a tether).

The estimate: "rubba shay'." It may also be a particle that cancels (kaffa) "rubba" and prepares it so that it can enter upon the verb, since it is not its nature to enter except upon nouns; and that is when there is no returning pronoun there, like the saying of the poet: (p-271)

"Rubbama awfaytu fi 'alamin tarfa'na thawbi shamalat" (Perhaps I have reached a high peak, where the north winds lift my garment).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Likewise "ma" enters upon "min" as a cancelling particle, as in his saying: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was among those who would move his lips," and like the saying of the poet:

"Wa-inna lamimma nadribu al-kabsha darbatan 'ala ra'sihi tulqi al-lisana mina al-fam" (Indeed we strike the ram a blow upon its head, so that the tongue is cast out of the mouth).

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the rule with "rubama" is that it enters upon the past verb, but here it enters upon the future, because these future verbs are the speech of Allah the Exalted, and since they are true and certain to occur, they take the place of the past that has occurred.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Rubba" may enter upon a past verb that is meant for the future, and it may enter in the reverse.

The apparent reading of "rubama" in this verse is that "ma" is a cancelling particle; thus said Abu 'Ali. He said: it is possible that it is a noun, and that "yawaddu" has a pronoun returning to it, the estimate being: "rubba waddin" or "a thing which those who disbelieved wish for, that they had been Muslims," and "law kanu muslimin" would be in apposition (badal) to "ma."

(p-272) A group said: the estimate of the verse is: "Perhaps there was someone whom those who disbelieved wished..." Abu 'Ali said: Sibawayh does not permit this, because "kana" is not elided according to him.

The interpreters differed about the time at which those who disbelieved will wish that they had been Muslims. One group said: it is at the moment of witnessing death in this world; this is related from al-Dahhak, and there is in it a point of consideration, since the disbeliever at that time has no certainty about the good state of the Muslims. Another group said: it is at the witnessing of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection; this was said by Mujahid, and this is clear, since the good state of the Muslims is evident, so they wish for it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is at their entry into the Fire and their knowledge of the entry of the believers into Paradise. For this saying an argument is made from a hadith narrated on this matter through the route of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, which is: "When Allah the Exalted brings the sinful Muslims into the Fire, the disbelievers look at them and say: 'Are not these from among the Muslims? What then did 'There is no god but Allah' avail them?' Then Allah the Exalted becomes angry at their saying, and says: 'Bring out from the Fire every Muslim!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Then those who disbelieved will wish that they had been Muslims.'" And their certainty in this is firmly established by the good state of the Muslims. So, from the standpoint of all this being one in every saying, "rubama" is for paucity, because they were in this world not wishing for Islam at all times; and from the standpoint of the abode of the Hereafter, their wish in it endures, so some people made this "rubama" for abundance, since whenever they remember his matter, they wish they had been Muslims.

And "law" in this verse is for wishing, and it may include the prevention of one thing due to the prevention of another, by an implied element clarified by the meaning, which is that they wished they had been Muslims so that they would be saved with the salvation whose barrier is that they were not Muslims.

(p-273) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among the lessons in this verse is the hadith of al-Wabisi, which is in the appendix of al-Amali, and its implication is that he apostatized and forgot the Qur'an except this verse.

His saying, the Exalted: "Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves" to the end of the verse, is a threat and an intimidation, and what is in it of conciliation is abrogated by the verse of the sword. His saying: "they will soon know" is a second threat. Al-Tabari related from some scholars that he said: the first is in this world, and the second in the Hereafter; how then can life be pleasant between these two threats? The meaning of His saying: "and let hope distract them" is: their hope in worldly things and their increase in them occupies them from reflection and belief in Allah and His Messenger.

The meaning of His saying: "We did not destroy any town except that..." to the end of the verse is: do not be impatient for their destruction; there is no town except that it will be destroyed at a term and a decree. The meaning of [ma'lum] is limited. The waw in His saying "wa-laha" is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "illa laha" without a waw. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: this waw is the one which indicates that the state following it in wording is in time before the state that precedes the waw, and from it is His saying, the Exalted: "until, when they reach it and its gates are opened" (al-Zumar: 73). The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 15, verse 1–5:

(p-269) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Hijr

This surah is Meccan.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieve will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them; they will soon know.﴾ ﴿We did not destroy any town except that it had a known decree.﴾ ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can it delay it.﴾

"Alif, Lam, Ra": the discussion of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of the surahs has already preceded. "Tilka" (these) may refer, according to some opinions, to the letters of the alphabet (huruf al-mu'jam). It is also possible that it refers to the wisdoms, lessons and the like that the verses of the Torah and the Gospel contained, and the Qur'an is conjoined to it. Mujahid and Qatada said: "the Book" in the verse is what was revealed of the books before the Qur'an. It is also possible that "the Book" is meant to be the Qur'an, and then the attribute is conjoined to it.

Nafi' and 'Asim read "rubama" with a light ba' (ب), and the rest read it with a shadda, except that Abu 'Amr read it both ways; both are dialects. It is related from Talha ibn Musarrif "rubbatama" with the addition of a ta', (p-270) and this is a dialect. "Rubama" is for paucity, though it may occasionally come for abundance. Some people said that this is from that, and from it is the line:

"Rubba ka'sin harraqta ya ibna Lu'ayy" (How many a cup you spilled, O son of Lu'ayy).

Al-Zajjaj denied that "rubba" comes for abundance.

The "ma" that "rubba" enters upon may be a indefinite noun in the sense of "shay'" (thing), and that is when there is in the speech a pronoun returning to it, like the saying of the poet:

"Rubbama takrahu al-nufusu mina al-amr lahu furjatun ka-hallil-iqal" (Perhaps the souls dislike a matter, for it there is a relief like the untying of a tether).

The estimate: "rubba shay'." It may also be a particle that cancels (kaffa) "rubba" and prepares it so that it can enter upon the verb, since it is not its nature to enter except upon nouns; and that is when there is no returning pronoun there, like the saying of the poet: (p-271)

"Rubbama awfaytu fi 'alamin tarfa'na thawbi shamalat" (Perhaps I have reached a high peak, where the north winds lift my garment).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Likewise "ma" enters upon "min" as a cancelling particle, as in his saying: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was among those who would move his lips," and like the saying of the poet:

"Wa-inna lamimma nadribu al-kabsha darbatan 'ala ra'sihi tulqi al-lisana mina al-fam" (Indeed we strike the ram a blow upon its head, so that the tongue is cast out of the mouth).

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: the rule with "rubama" is that it enters upon the past verb, but here it enters upon the future, because these future verbs are the speech of Allah the Exalted, and since they are true and certain to occur, they take the place of the past that has occurred.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Rubba" may enter upon a past verb that is meant for the future, and it may enter in the reverse.

The apparent reading of "rubama" in this verse is that "ma" is a cancelling particle; thus said Abu 'Ali. He said: it is possible that it is a noun, and that "yawaddu" has a pronoun returning to it, the estimate being: "rubba waddin" or "a thing which those who disbelieved wish for, that they had been Muslims," and "law kanu muslimin" would be in apposition (badal) to "ma."

(p-272) A group said: the estimate of the verse is: "Perhaps there was someone whom those who disbelieved wished..." Abu 'Ali said: Sibawayh does not permit this, because "kana" is not elided according to him.

The interpreters differed about the time at which those who disbelieved will wish that they had been Muslims. One group said: it is at the moment of witnessing death in this world; this is related from al-Dahhak, and there is in it a point of consideration, since the disbeliever at that time has no certainty about the good state of the Muslims. Another group said: it is at the witnessing of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection; this was said by Mujahid, and this is clear, since the good state of the Muslims is evident, so they wish for it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is at their entry into the Fire and their knowledge of the entry of the believers into Paradise. For this saying an argument is made from a hadith narrated on this matter through the route of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, which is: "When Allah the Exalted brings the sinful Muslims into the Fire, the disbelievers look at them and say: 'Are not these from among the Muslims? What then did 'There is no god but Allah' avail them?' Then Allah the Exalted becomes angry at their saying, and says: 'Bring out from the Fire every Muslim!' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Then those who disbelieved will wish that they had been Muslims.'" And their certainty in this is firmly established by the good state of the Muslims. So, from the standpoint of all this being one in every saying, "rubama" is for paucity, because they were in this world not wishing for Islam at all times; and from the standpoint of the abode of the Hereafter, their wish in it endures, so some people made this "rubama" for abundance, since whenever they remember his matter, they wish they had been Muslims.

And "law" in this verse is for wishing, and it may include the prevention of one thing due to the prevention of another, by an implied element clarified by the meaning, which is that they wished they had been Muslims so that they would be saved with the salvation whose barrier is that they were not Muslims.

(p-273) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Among the lessons in this verse is the hadith of al-Wabisi, which is in the appendix of al-Amali, and its implication is that he apostatized and forgot the Qur'an except this verse.

[p-274]

The Most High said:

﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are surely a madman!"﴾ ﴿"If only you would bring us the angels, if you are of the truthful."﴾ ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and then they would not be reprieved.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians.﴾ ﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ ﴿And no messenger came to them but that they mocked him.﴾

The pronoun in "qalu" (they said) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It is narrated that those who said this were 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and their like. Al-A'mash (d. 148 AH), a reciter, read: "O you to whom the Reminder has been cast" (ألقي). Their saying, ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾, is spoken in a tone of derision, meaning "according to your claim and your assertion." This form of address is like saying to an ignorant man who wants to speak on matters he does not understand: "O scholar, you do not perform ablution well."

"Lawma" (لوما) has the meaning of "lawla" (لولا, "if only" / "why not"). It is then an exhortation (tahdid), as in this verse. It may also indicate the prevention of one thing due to the existence of another, as Ibn Muqbil said:

Were it not for modesty, and were it not for religion, I would have blamed you both
For some of what is in you both, since you blamed my faults.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read ما تنزل الملائكة (*mā tanzilu al-malā'ikah*) with a fatha on the ta and the nominative case (raf') for "al-malā'ikah," meaning "the angels descend." 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read it with a damma on the ta; this is also the reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read نُنَزِّلُ (*nunazzilu*), with the first person plural of majesty, and al-malā'ikata in the accusative case; this is the reading of Talha ibn Musarrif.

As for His saying ﴿except with truth﴾, Mujahid said: the meaning is "with the message and with punishment."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (Ibn 'Atiyya), may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning is: as is required and as is due, of revelation and of the benefits which Allah shows to His servants, not according to the proposals of a disbeliever, nor by the choice of an objector. Then He mentioned Allah's custom regarding the nations: that He did not bring them any sign of their own proposing unless punishment followed it if they did not believe. It is as if the statement means: "We do not send down the angels except with a truth and a obligation, not by your proposal." Also, if they had descended, they would not have been granted respite from punishment after that. The word "nazrah" (نظرة) means delay, and the meaning is: this does not happen, since it was in Allah's knowledge that among them are those who will believe, or who will beget those who will believe.

His saying, Most High: ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder﴾ is a response to those who derided, in their saying ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾. This is like when a man says to you in derision, "O you of great station," and you reply to him, in refutation and rebuke: "Yes, I am of great station," and then you continue your speech. Consider this carefully. As for His saying ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾, one group said: the pronoun in "lahu" (له) refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: We protect him from your harm and safeguard him from your plotting and other things. Al-Tabari mentioned this opinion without attributing it. Within this assurance, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was protected until Allah made the Law prevail through him and his term came. Another group, which is the majority, said: the pronoun in "lahu" refers to the Qur'an. Mujahid and Qatada said this, and the meaning is: We guard it from being altered or changed, as happened with the other revealed books. The apparent meaning of the Qur'anic verses, however, is that they altered the wording, and placing the hand on the verse of stoning is in effect altering the wording. It has been said: "We are its guardians" means by its being stored in the chests of men. The meanings are close. Qatada said: this verse is similar to His saying, Most High: ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾ [Fussilat: 42].

His saying, Most High: ﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you﴾ is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) and an offering of an example. We have already sent messengers before, among the sects of the earlier peoples, and this was their way of mocking the messengers. His saying ﴿We sent before you﴾ requires "messengers" (رسلا) to be understood, and then their mention is omitted because an apparent indication in the speech points to it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 15, verses 12–15:

His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Thus do We insert it into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ ﴿They do not believe in it, though the precedent of the former peoples has passed.﴾ ﴿And even if We opened to them a gate from the sky, and they continued to ascend through it,﴾ ﴿they would say, "Our eyes have only been intoxicated; rather, we are a people bewitched."﴾

The pronoun refers to mockery or polytheism and the like. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Zayd. In this case the pronoun in "bihi" refers to that very thing, and the bā' is the bā' of causality, meaning: they do not believe because of their polytheism and mockery. His saying, "they do not believe in it," is then in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is also possible that the pronoun in "naslukuhu" refers to the "preserved Reminder" mentioned earlier, which is the Qur'an, meaning: rejected, dismissed, and mocked, We insert it into the hearts of the criminals; the pronoun in "bihi" then also refers to it, meaning: they do not give it credence. It is also possible that the pronoun in "naslukuhu" refers to mockery and polytheism, while the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an, so the reference of the two pronouns differs on this reading. The meaning in all of this is that each part looks to the others.

"Naslukuhu" means "We insert it" (nadkhuluhu). One says: "salaktu al-rajul fi al-amr" when you make a man enter into a matter. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I was the stout defender of your opponent, I did not flee, / While they had put you into a grave matter."

And from it is the saying of another:

"Until, when they had driven them into a narrow place, / Scattering them as the camel-drivers drive the wild asses."

And from it is the saying of Abu Wajza describing wild asses:

"Until they entered the hooves among them into a sandy tract / of the offspring of the one who traverses the horizons, the striped one."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is also read "nuslikuhu" with a damma on the nūn and a kasra on the lām. The "criminals" in this verse are intended to mean the unbelievers of Quraysh and the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

His saying, Exalted is He, "They do not believe in it," is a general statement whose meaning is particular to those upon whom a seal has been set. His saying, "though the precedent of the former peoples has passed," means: upon this same course. One says: "salaktu al-rajul fi al-amr" and "aslaktuhu," with the same meaning. It is also transmitted: "Until, when they had driven them (aslakuhum) into a narrow place."

His saying, Exalted is He, "And even if We opened to them," the pronoun refers to Quraysh and the unbelievers of the age upon whom the seal has been set. The pronoun in His saying "fazallu" (they continued) may refer back to them, and this is more emphatic regarding their obstinacy; this is the interpretation of al-Hasan. "Ya'rujun" means "they ascend." al-A'mash and Abu Haywa read "ya'rijun" with a kasra on the rā'. The ma'arij are the stairways, and from it comes al-mi'raj (the ascent). From it is the saying of Kuthayyir:

"To a noble ancestry, which the man's forefathers built before him, / his father has in it ladders of steps."

It is also possible that it refers to the angels, because of their saying: "Why do you not bring us the angels?" [al-Hijr: 7]. It is as if Allah, Exalted is He, said: "Even if they saw the angels ascending and moving freely through an open gate in the sky, they would not believe." This is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The Seven Readers, other than Ibn Kathir, read "sukkirat" with a damma on the sīn and a shadda on the kāf. Ibn Kathir alone read it with the kāf lightened, and this is the reading of Mujahid. Ibn al-Zuhri read it with a fatha on the sīn and a lightened kāf, based on the verb being active. Aban ibn Taghlib read "suḥḥirat abṣāruna" (our eyes have been bewitched). The saying, "Rather, we are a people bewitched," moves to a greater degree of the magic of the intellect. The Arabs say: "sakarat al-rih tuskaru sukuran" when the wind became still and did not pass through in the way it previously was accustomed to. They also say: "sakira al-rajul min al-sharab yaskaru sukran" when his condition changed, he became still, and he could no longer act in what a person is capable of acting in. From this meaning comes the saying: "a drunkard does not decide," meaning he does not conclude any matter. The Arabs also say: "sakarat al-fatq fi majari al-ma' sakran" when one blocks the breach in the water channels and turns the water away from it, so it does not pass in its proper course.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for this word, "sukkirat" with the kāf doubled, if it derives from the intoxication of drink, or from the stillness of the wind, then it is a verb made transitive by doubling. If it derives from blocking the channels of water, then its doubling is for intensification, not for transitivity, since the unaugmented form of it is already transitive. Abu Hatim preferred this reading, because "al-absar" is plural, and doubling is more common with the plural, as in His saying: "their gates opened for them" [Sad: 50]. As for one who reads "sakirat" with a damma on the sīn and a lightened kāf: if the word derives from "sakira al-ma'" (the water was blocked), then it is a transitive verb; and if it derives from the intoxication of drink or the stillness of the wind, then we must assume the verb has been passivized until we make it transitive, and this verb will be of the type: "raja'a Zayd" and "raja'ahu ghayruhu" (Zayd returned, and another returned him), and "ghārat al-'ayn" and "gharaha al-rajul" (the eye sank and a man sank it). So one would say: "sakira al-rajul" and "sakarahu ghayruhu," and "sakarat al-rih" and "sakaraha shay' ghayruha." The meaning of this statement from them is: our eyes have been altered from what they were, so they no longer give us the realities of things as they used to. Some exegetes rendered this word as: "our eyes have been covered" (ghushiya 'ala absarina); others said: "our eyes have been blinded" ('ummiyat absaruna). This and similar renderings are interpretation by meaning, not tied to the word. It is also said that these people, who see, refer to the ascent of the angels or the ascent of themselves, after their saying: "Our eyes have only been intoxicated." Rather, we have been bewitched, until we do not comprehend things as they should be comprehended; that is, magic has been directed upon us.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 15, verses 16–21:**

The Exalted said:

﴿And We have placed constellations in the sky and adorned it for the beholders.﴾ ﴿And We have guarded it from every accursed devil.﴾ ﴿Except one who eavesdrops, and he is pursued by a clear flaming fire.﴾ ﴿And the earth – We spread it out, cast into it firm mountains, and caused to grow in it every thing in balance.﴾ ﴿And We have made for you therein means of livelihood, and for those whom you do not provide for.﴾ ﴿And there is nothing but that its treasuries are with Us, and We send it down only in a known measure.﴾

Because He mentioned that they would, if they saw the aforementioned sign in the sky, persist in their denial, He followed it with this verse. It is as if He said: "Indeed, in the sky there are other signs set up besides this one that is mentioned. Their disbelief in them and their turning away from them is persistence and arrogant defiance."

The *burūj* (constellations, or mansions) are its stations; its singular is *burj*. It is so called because of its prominence and clarity. From the same root is *tabarruj al-mar'ah* (a woman's display), meaning her showing and exposing herself. The Arabs say, "*barija al-shay'*" when a thing becomes apparent and rises high.

The guarding of the sky is by pelting with shooting stars, as is contained in the sound hadiths. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the devils approach the sky in groups." He said: "A rebellious one among them separates off, ascends, listens, and is struck by a shooting star. He then says to his companions, panting: 'Indeed, such-and-such a matter is occurring,' and the devil adds to it, and they convey it to the soothsayers, who add a hundred lies to the one word." And similar to this hadith.

Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him) said: "The shooting stars wound and harm, but do not kill." Al-Hasan said: "They kill." The hadiths contain what indicates that the pelting existed in the pre-Islamic period (*jāhiliyyah*), but it intensified at the time of Islam, and it guarded the sky with complete protection. Al-Zajjaj said: "It did not occur except after the Prophet (ﷺ), as evidence that poets were not likened to it in speed except after Islam." Al-Zahrawi reported from Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi that he said: "We did not see the pelting with stars before Islam."

*Rajīm* means *marjūm* (pelted), an *fa'īl* in the sense of *maf'ūl*. It is either from the pelting with shooting stars, or from *al-rajm* which means reviling and blaming. It is said: "*tabi'tu al-rajul*" and "*ittaba'tuhu*" with the same meaning. *Illā* is in the sense of *lākin* (but); this is one opinion. The apparent view is that the exception (*istithnā'*) is from the guarding. Muhammad ibn Yahya reported from his father: "*Illā man istaraqa al-sam'*" means that it (the sky) was not guarded from him; this was related by al-Zahrawi.

As for His saying, ﴿And the earth – We spread it out﴾: it is narrated in a hadith that the earth used to sway with its inhabitants as a ship sways, so God, blessed and exalted, made it firm with mountains. It is said: *rasā al-shay'* means "it settled" when it became firm and steady. As for His saying *mawzūn* (in balance): the majority said its meaning is: determined and delimited by intention and will. The weighing in this sense is metaphorical. Ibn Zayd said: what is intended is what is literally weighed, such as gold, silver, and other things that are weighed.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: The first is more general and better.

*Ma'āyish* is the plural of *ma'īshah*. Al-A'mash recited it with a hamza, and likewise Kharija reported from Nafi'. The correct form is to omit the hamza, because the root of the *yā'* in *ma'īshah* is movement, so the plural returns it to its origin, unlike *madīnah* and *madā'in*.

As for His saying ﴿and for those whom you do not provide for﴾: *man* may be in the accusative position in three ways. The first is that it is conjoined to *ma'āyish*, as if God enumerated the blessings in livelihoods, which are what is eaten and worn, and then enumerated the blessings in animals, slaves, estates, and other things from which people benefit, and for which their provision is not upon them. The second is that *man* is conjoined to the position of the pronoun in *lakum* (for you); the meaning is: "We have made life for you and made life for other nations of animals." On this view, the verse contains an admonition and a presentation of a sign. The third is that *man* is in the accusative by an implied verb required by the apparent sense; its estimate is: "And We have made live those for whom you do not provide." *Man* may also be in the genitive position, conjoined to the pronoun in *lakum*. This is a difficult point in grammar, because conjoining to a pronoun in the genitive is ugly. So it is as if He said: "And for whom you do not provide, and from whom you benefit."

As for His saying ﴿And there is nothing but that its treasuries are with Us﴾: Ibn Jurayj said: "This is specifically the rain."

The judge Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: It is fitting that it be more general than this regarding many created things. *Khazā'in* (treasuries) are the containing places. The apparent meaning is that water, wind, and the like exist as created things. This is evident in the statement regarding the wind: "It rose up over the treasuries, and there opened from it only the size of a ring's hole; had it been the size of a bull's nostril, it would have destroyed the earth," and other such evidences. Some people held that their being in God's power is their being stored, so when God wills He brings them into existence. This too is apparent in many things, and it necessarily applies to accidents if we generalize the word *shay'* (thing). However it is, power encompasses it and perfects it.

As for His saying, ﴿and We send it down﴾: whatever is rain or the like, sending down (*inzāl*) is properly applied to it. Whatever is other than that, its bringing into existence and enabling people to benefit from it is "sending down" in a figurative sense. Al-A'mash recited: "*wa-mā nursiluhu illā bi-qadarin ma'lūm*" (and We send it only in a known measure). As for His saying ﴿in a known measure﴾: it was reported from Ibn Mas'ud and others that there is no year more abundant in rain than another year, but God sends it down in some places and not in others.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 15, verses 22–27:**

(p-282) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We send the winds fertilizing, then We send down water from the sky and give it to you to drink, and you are not its storers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the inheritors.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly known those of you who go before, and We have certainly known those who remain behind.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord — it is He who will gather them. Indeed, He is Wise and Knowing.﴾ ﴿And We certainly created man from clay of black mud altered.﴾ ﴿And the jinn We had created before from the fire of scorching wind.﴾

It is said: the she-camel and the tree were *luqqiḥat* (impregnated/fertilized), so it is *lāqiḥah* when it has conceived. The winds fertilize the trees and the clouds. So the proper description of the wind is that it is *mulaqqiḥah* (causing fertilization), not *lāqiḥah* (being fertilized). The description of the winds as *lawāqiḥ* (fertilizing) may be interpreted in four ways. The first, and the best of them, is that making it *lāqiḥah* is literal. This is because some winds carry punishment, harm or fire, and some carry mercy, rain, victory or other things. So they bear what Power has loaded upon them, or what they have gathered from the air, the dust or the water over which they pass. Thus they are *lāqiḥah* in this sense, although they also fertilize others and deliver their benefit to them. The Arabs call the south wind *al-ḥāmil* (the bearing one) and *al-lāqiḥah*, and they call the north wind *al-ḥā'il* (the barren one), *al-'aqīm* (the sterile one) and *Maḥwah*, because it erases the clouds. Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The south wind is from Paradise, and it is the fertilizing winds that Allah mentioned, and in it are benefits for people." From this is the saying of al-Ṭirimmāḥ:

*Restless for the branches of the winds, for one that fertilizes among them and one that does not.*

And the saying of Abū Wajzah:

.......................

*From the lineage of Jawwābat al-Āfāq…*

(p-283) So he made it bearing offspring.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This goes out on the basis that they are *mulaqqiḥah*, so there is no proof in it.

The second: that describing them as *lawāqiḥ* is from the pattern of their saying "a sleeping night" (*laylun nā'im*), meaning there is sleep in it and with it, and "a stormy day" (*yawmun 'āṣif*), and the like. This is by way of metaphor (*majāz*). The third: that the winds are described as *lawāqiḥ* in the sense of attribution (*nasab*), meaning possessing fertilization, like the saying of al-Nābighah:

*Leave me alone for a worry, O Umaymah, troubled one…*

meaning: possessing trouble. The fourth: that *lawāqiḥ* is the plural of *mulaqqiḥah* with its extra letters removed, so it is as if it were *laqiḥah*, and he made its plural as one makes the plural of *lāqiḥah*. Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

*Labbayka Yazīd, the humble one for a dispute… and the disheveled one of those whom the stumbling ones have made stumble.*

Indeed, it was the stumbling ones who made him stumble. In this manner Abū 'Ubaydah explained it in his saying: "*lawāqiḥ mala-qiḥ*," and likewise the expression for it in the Book of al-Bukhārī: "*lawāqiḥ malāqiḥ mulaqqiḥah*."

(p-284) The majority (*al-Jumhūr*) read "*al-riyāḥ*" in the plural. The Kufans, Ḥamzah, Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif, al-A'mash and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read "*al-rīḥ*" in the singular, and it is for the genus, so it carries the meaning of the plural. al-Ṭabarī illustrated it with their saying: "a shirt of *akhlāq*" (worn-out), and "a land of *aghfāl*" (barren, untilled).

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is from the point of view that it is many parts that collectively describe it, so likewise "a *rīḥ lawāqiḥ*" because its blowing is scattered. Likewise "a *dār bilāqi'*," meaning every place in it is a desolate plain. Al-A'mash said: In the reading of 'Abd Allah there is "*wa arsalnā al-riyāḥa talqaḥ*." It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The wind is from the breath of the All-Merciful." The meaning of the annexation here is the annexation of creation to the Creator, as He said: "from My spirit." The meaning of "from the breath of the All-Merciful" is from His giving relief and removing distress and hardships. This goes out on the basis that they are *mulaqqiḥah*, so there is no proof in it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 15, verses 28–33**

The Exalted said:

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am creating a human being from clay, from black mud altered into shape."﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] soul, then fall down to him in prostration.﴾ ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely.﴾ ﴿Except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrated.﴾ ﴿[Allah] said, "O Iblis, what is [the matter] with you that you are not among those who prostrate?"﴾ ﴿He said, "I would never prostrate to a human being whom You created from clay, from black mud altered into shape."﴾

The word إذْ (idh, "when") is in the accusative case by virtue of an implied verb whose estimated form is: "Remember when your Lord said." The word البَشَرُ (al-bashar, "human being") here refers to Adam. It derives from البَشَرَة (al-bashara, "the skin"), which, according to the most well-known view, is the outer surface of the skin. From this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Keep the skin clean." It is also said that al-bashara is the layer adjacent to the flesh. From this is the proverb: "Only the hide that has the skin is blamed," because that layer is the one that shows (yubashshiru) [the effects]. Allah informed the angels of something that astonished them, for they had been created from light, and so they were fine bodies. He informed them that He would create a living bodily being with skin, and that He would create him from clay. The words بِشْر (bishr, "cheerfulness") and بِشَارَة (bisharah, "good news") also originally derive from al-bashara, because they become apparent upon it.

The word سَوَّيْتُهُ (sawwaytuhu, "I have proportioned him") means: I completed him and perfected him, until his parts were balanced as they should be. His saying ﴿of My [created] soul﴾ is an attribution of creation and ownership to the Creator and Owner: that is, of the soul that belongs to Me. The word al-rūḥ (soul) here is generic (li-l-jins). His saying "fa-qaʿū" (fall down) comes from waqaʿa yaqaʿu, and the qāf is vowelled with fatḥa because of the guttural letter (ḥarf al-ḥalq). This wording strengthens the view that the prostration of the angels was in the familiar sense known to us, and not, as some people have said, mere submission, acceptance, or a gesture. They compared it to the verse of the poet:

*So both of them fell down, and she bowed her head, as a Christian woman prostrates, one who has not inclined to the true faith (lam taḥannif).*

This line resembles one in which prostration carries the familiar meaning known to us. Al-Tabari, in his tafsir of this verse, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Allah created angels and commanded them to prostrate to Adam, but they refused. So He sent fire upon them, and it burned them. Then He created others, and it was the same. Then He created others and commanded them to prostrate, and they obeyed, except Iblis, for he was among the first [group]." His saying "among the first" may mean: among the first in their state and their disbelief. It may also mean: [that he was] among those who remained from them.

His saying ﴿all of them entirely﴾ is, according to Sibawayh, an emphasis upon an emphasis, where the latter includes what the former included. Others said: if one stopped at "kulluhum" (all of them), it would be suitable for an exception, and it would also suit the sense of hyperbole, even if some of them had not prostrated. This is like one who says, "All people know such-and-such," intending that the matter mentioned is well known. When he says "ajma'ūn" (entirely), the possibility that some of them remained is removed, and the statement requires that all of them prostrated. Al-Mubarrad said: if one stopped at "kulluhum," it would be possible that their prostrations occurred on many occasions; but when he says "ajma'ūn," it indicates that they prostrated on one single occasion.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Mubarrad's view has been objected to on the grounds that he made His saying "ajma'ūn" a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), in the sense of "gathered together." On this view, "ajma'ūn" would have to be nearly indefinite, though it is definite, because it obliges the following of definite forms. The reading with the nominative (raf') rejects his saying.

As for His saying ﴿except Iblis﴾: it is said that this is an exception from the first group, and it is said that he is not from the first group. This rests on the disagreement about Iblis: is he among the angels or not? The apparent meaning of many ḥadīths and of this verse is that he is among the angels, because Allah commanded the angels to prostrate, and if Iblis had not been among the angels he would not have sinned by abandoning the prostration. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 15, verses 28–33**

The Exalted said:

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am creating a human being from clay, from black mud altered into shape."﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My [created] soul, then fall down to him in prostration.﴾ ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely.﴾ ﴿Except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrated.﴾ ﴿[Allah] said, "O Iblis, what is [the matter] with you that you are not among those who prostrate?"﴾ ﴿He said, "I would never prostrate to a human being whom You created from clay, from black mud altered into shape."﴾

The word إذْ (idh, "when") is in the accusative case by virtue of an implied verb whose estimated form is: "Remember when your Lord said." The word البَشَرُ (al-bashar, "human being") here refers to Adam. It derives from البَشَرَة (al-bashara, "the skin"), which, according to the most well-known view, is the outer surface of the skin. From this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Keep the skin clean." It is also said that al-bashara is the layer adjacent to the flesh. From this is the proverb: "Only the hide that has the skin is blamed," because that layer is the one that shows (yubashshiru) [the effects]. Allah informed the angels of something that astonished them, for they had been created from light, and so they were fine bodies. He informed them that He would create a living bodily being with skin, and that He would create him from clay. The words بِشْر (bishr, "cheerfulness") and بِشَارَة (bisharah, "good news") also originally derive from al-bashara, because they become apparent upon it.

The word سَوَّيْتُهُ (sawwaytuhu, "I have proportioned him") means: I completed him and perfected him, until his parts were balanced as they should be. His saying ﴿of My [created] soul﴾ is an attribution of creation and ownership to the Creator and Owner: that is, of the soul that belongs to Me. The word al-rūḥ (soul) here is generic (li-l-jins). His saying "fa-qaʿū" (fall down) comes from waqaʿa yaqaʿu, and the qāf is vowelled with fatḥa because of the guttural letter (ḥarf al-ḥalq). This wording strengthens the view that the prostration of the angels was in the familiar sense known to us, and not, as some people have said, mere submission, acceptance, or a gesture. They compared it to the verse of the poet:

*So both of them fell down, and she bowed her head, as a Christian woman prostrates, one who has not inclined to the true faith (lam taḥannif).*

This line resembles one in which prostration carries the familiar meaning known to us. Al-Tabari, in his tafsir of this verse, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Allah created angels and commanded them to prostrate to Adam, but they refused. So He sent fire upon them, and it burned them. Then He created others, and it was the same. Then He created others and commanded them to prostrate, and they obeyed, except Iblis, for he was among the first [group]." His saying "among the first" may mean: among the first in their state and their disbelief. It may also mean: [that he was] among those who remained from them.

His saying ﴿all of them entirely﴾ is, according to Sibawayh, an emphasis upon an emphasis, where the latter includes what the former included. Others said: if one stopped at "kulluhum" (all of them), it would be suitable for an exception, and it would also suit the sense of hyperbole, even if some of them had not prostrated. This is like one who says, "All people know such-and-such," intending that the matter mentioned is well known. When he says "ajma'ūn" (entirely), the possibility that some of them remained is removed, and the statement requires that all of them prostrated. Al-Mubarrad said: if one stopped at "kulluhum," it would be possible that their prostrations occurred on many occasions; but when he says "ajma'ūn," it indicates that they prostrated on one single occasion.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Mubarrad's view has been objected to on the grounds that he made His saying "ajma'ūn" a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), in the sense of "gathered together." On this view, "ajma'ūn" would have to be nearly indefinite, though it is definite, because it obliges the following of definite forms. The reading with the nominative (raf') rejects his saying.

This rests on the disagreement about Iblis: is he among the angels or not? قَالَ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ:

﴿قالَ فاخْرُجْ مِنها فَإنَّكَ رَجِيمٌ﴾ ﴿He said: "Get out of it, for you are accursed."﴾ ﴿وَإنَّ عَلَيْكَ اللَعْنَةَ إلى يَوْمِ الدِينِ﴾ ﴿And indeed upon you is the curse until the Day of Recompense.﴾ ﴿قالَ رَبِّ فَأنْظِرْنِي إلى يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, then give me respite until the day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿قالَ فَإنَّكَ مِنَ المُنْظَرِينَ﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed you are among those given respite,"﴾ ﴿إلى يَوْمِ الوَقْتِ المَعْلُومِ﴾ ﴿until the day of the appointed time.﴾ ﴿قالَ رَبِّ بِما أغْوَيْتَنِي لأُزَيِّنَنَّ لَهم في الأرْضِ ولأُغْوِيَنَّهم أجْمَعِينَ﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will surely mislead them all,"﴾ ﴿إلا عِبادَكَ مِنهُمُ المُخْلَصِينَ﴾ ﴿except Your sincere servants among them.﴾ ﴿قالَ هَذا صِراطٌ عَلَيَّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a path that leads straight to Me."﴾ [p. 292] ﴿إنَّ عِبادِي لَيْسَ لَكَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُلْطانٌ إلا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ مِنَ الغاوِينَ﴾ ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators.﴾ ﴿وَإنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمَوْعِدُهم أجْمَعِينَ﴾ ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all.﴾ ﴿لَها سَبْعَةُ أبْوابٍ لِكُلِّ بابٍ مِنهم جُزْءٌ مَقْسُومٌ﴾ ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a designated portion of them.﴾

The pronoun in "مِنها" refers to Paradise, even though it has not been mentioned, since it is implied within the narrative. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the category of angels. "الرَجِيمُ" means the accursed, i.e., the one stoned with words and abuse. "﴿يَوْمِ الدِينِ﴾" means the Day of Recompense (al-jaza'). From this is the saying of the poet:

"Nothing remained but the enemies; we repaid them as they had repaid [us]."

Iblis asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection, and God granted him respite until an appointed time. Scholars differed about it. It was said: until the Day of Resurrection, meaning he will be the last of creation to die; this was stated by al-Tabari and others. It was also said: until an unspecified and undetermined time, neither the Resurrection nor anything else, and its knowledge is with God alone. It was also said: rather, his respite was until the Day of Badr, and that he was killed on the Day of Badr. This, although it has been related, is weak. "Al-Munzar" means the one delayed. His saying "My Lord," despite his disbelief, is explained as an acknowledgment of lordship (rububiyya) and of creation, which is the apparent condition of him and what the verses and hadiths imply about him; yet this does not negate the fundamental nature of his disbelief.

As for his saying ﴿بِما أغْوَيْتَنِي﴾ (because You have led me astray), Abu 'Ubayda and others said: "He swore by the act of misleading," as though he placed it in the position of saying, "My Lord, by Your power over me and Your decree." It is also possible that it means "because of," as though he said: "My Lord, by God, I will mislead them because of Your misleading me, on account of it and in return for it." It is also possible that the meaning is an expression of resolve from him and an emphasis on earnestness, i.e., "in this state of mine and my distance from good, by God, I will surely act and surely mislead." The meaning of ﴿لأُزَيِّنَنَّ لَهم في الأرْضِ﴾ is: [I will make attractive to them] the desires and sins. The pronoun in "لَهُمْ" refers to the descendants of Adam, even though they have not been mentioned; the narrative as a whole, wherever it occurs in full, includes them. "Al-Ighwa'" means misguidance (al-idlal).

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, and al-A'raj read "المُخْلَصِينَ" with a fatha on the lam, meaning those whom You have made sincere (akhlaṣtahum) for Your worship and Your piety. The majority read it with a kasra on the lam, meaning those who sincerely held faith in You and in Your messengers.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿قالَ هَذا صِراطٌ عَلَيَّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾, the speaker is God, may He be blessed and exalted. It is possible that this is conveyed through an intermediary. al-Dahhak, Humayd, al-Nakha'i, Abu Raja', Ibn Sirin, Qatada, Qays ibn 'Abbad, Mujahid, and others read "عَلِيٌّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ" (lofty and straight), from loftiness and exaltedness. According to this reading, the demonstrative "هَذا" refers to sincerity. When Iblis was excepted from those who were sincere, God said to him: "This sincerity is an elevated, straight path, which you, by your misleading, cannot reach its people." The majority of readers read "عَلَيَّ" with a shadda and a fatha on the yaʾ; according to this reading, the demonstrative "هَذا" refers to the division of people into deviators and sincere ones. When Iblis divided people into these two categories, God said to him: "This is a path leading to Me," i.e., this is a matter whose outcome is to Me, and the Arabs say, "Your way in this matter is upon so-and-so," meaning the consideration of your affair belongs to him. This is similar to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿إنَّ رَبَّكَ لَبِالمِرْصادِ﴾ [al-Fajr: 14] ("Indeed your Lord is ever watchful"). According to this reading, the verse is a statement that includes a threat.

Then He began to inform about the safety of His righteous servants from Iblis, and addressed him, saying that he has no proof over them and no power.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of His saying "My servants" is specific to the people of faith and piety, not the general creation. Accordingly, ﴿إلا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ is an exception from something other than the first clause. The meaning is: "But whoever follows you among the deviators has authority over them." If we take "servants" in a general sense, including the worshippers among people, since God did not grant Iblis any authority over anyone, then we consider the exception to be of a lesser quantity in terms of number, since the disbelievers have no measure. The first view is more correct. The purpose is only to avoid falling into the exception of the majority from the minority, although the jurists have permitted it. Abu al-Ma'ali said: it is not known in Arabic usage, and this verse is the best of what its permitters have cited as evidence.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

They have no proof from the verse according to what I have explained.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿وَإنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمَوْعِدُهُمْ﴾ means the place where they will gather. A "mawʿid" relates to both time and place, and sometimes the place is mentioned without specifying the time of the appointment. "Ajma'in" is an emphasis, and it carries the sense of a circumstantial (ḥāl). His saying ﴿لَها سَبْعَةُ أبْوابٍ﴾: it was said that the Fire in its entirety consists of seven layers (aṭbāq), the highest of which is Jahannam, then Laẓā, then al-Ḥuṭama, then al-Saʿir, then Saqar, then al-Jaḥīm, in which is Abu Jahl, then al-Hawiya; and that in each layer of it there is a gate. Thus, according to this view, the gates are some above others. In this verse, He referred to the Fire as a whole by Jahannam, since it is the most famous of its abodes and the first of them, and it is the place of the disobedient believers who do not dwell eternally in it; for this reason it was narrated that Jahannam will be destroyed and will decay. It was also said: the Fire consists of layers as we mentioned, but the seven gates are all in Jahannam on one level, and from each gate one descends to the layer to which it leads. I have abridged what the exegetes mentioned about the distances between the gates, about the air of the Fire, and about the manner of the condition, since these are numerous sayings most of which lack support; they fall within the realm of the permissible, and God's power is greater than these. May God protect us from His Fire and cover us with His mercy by His bounty.

As for His saying "juz'," the majority read it with a hamza. Ibn Shihab read it with a damma on the zay, and a group read "juzz" with a shadda on the zay without a hamza, which is the reading of Ibn al-Qa'qa'.

﴿قالَ فاخْرُجْ مِنها فَإنَّكَ رَجِيمٌ﴾ ﴿He said: "Get out of it, for you are accursed."﴾ ﴿وَإنَّ عَلَيْكَ اللَعْنَةَ إلى يَوْمِ الدِينِ﴾ ﴿And indeed upon you is the curse until the Day of Recompense.﴾ ﴿قالَ رَبِّ فَأنْظِرْنِي إلى يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, then give me respite until the day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿قالَ فَإنَّكَ مِنَ المُنْظَرِينَ﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed you are among those given respite,"﴾ ﴿إلى يَوْمِ الوَقْتِ المَعْلُومِ﴾ ﴿until the day of the appointed time.﴾ ﴿قالَ رَبِّ بِما أغْوَيْتَنِي لأُزَيِّنَنَّ لَهم في الأرْضِ ولأُغْوِيَنَّهم أجْمَعِينَ﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely make [evil] attractive to them on earth and will surely mislead them all,"﴾ ﴿إلا عِبادَكَ مِنهُمُ المُخْلَصِينَ﴾ ﴿except Your sincere servants among them.﴾ ﴿قالَ هَذا صِراطٌ عَلَيَّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾ ﴿He said: "This is a path that leads straight to Me."﴾ [p. 292] ﴿إنَّ عِبادِي لَيْسَ لَكَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُلْطانٌ إلا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ مِنَ الغاوِينَ﴾ ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators.﴾ ﴿وَإنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمَوْعِدُهم أجْمَعِينَ﴾ ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all.﴾ ﴿لَها سَبْعَةُ أبْوابٍ لِكُلِّ بابٍ مِنهم جُزْءٌ مَقْسُومٌ﴾ ﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a designated portion of them.﴾

The pronoun in "مِنها" refers to Paradise, even though it has not been mentioned, since it is implied within the narrative. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the category of angels. "الرَجِيمُ" means the accursed, i.e., the one stoned with words and abuse. "﴿يَوْمِ الدِينِ﴾" means the Day of Recompense (al-jaza'). From this is the saying of the poet:

"Nothing remained but the enemies; we repaid them as they had repaid [us]."

Iblis asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection, and God granted him respite until an appointed time. Scholars differed about it. It was said: until the Day of Resurrection, meaning he will be the last of creation to die; this was stated by al-Tabari and others. It was also said: until an unspecified and undetermined time, neither the Resurrection nor anything else, and its knowledge is with God alone. It was also said: rather, his respite was until the Day of Badr, and that he was killed on the Day of Badr. This, although it has been related, is weak. "Al-Munzar" means the one delayed. His saying "My Lord," despite his disbelief, is explained as an acknowledgment of lordship (rububiyya) and of creation, which is the apparent condition of him and what the verses and hadiths imply about him; yet this does not negate the fundamental nature of his disbelief.

As for his saying ﴿بِما أغْوَيْتَنِي﴾ (because You have led me astray), Abu 'Ubayda and others said: "He swore by the act of misleading," as though he placed it in the position of saying, "My Lord, by Your power over me and Your decree." It is also possible that it means "because of," as though he said: "My Lord, by God, I will mislead them because of Your misleading me, on account of it and in return for it." It is also possible that the meaning is an expression of resolve from him and an emphasis on earnestness, i.e., "in this state of mine and my distance from good, by God, I will surely act and surely mislead." The meaning of ﴿لأُزَيِّنَنَّ لَهم في الأرْضِ﴾ is: [I will make attractive to them] the desires and sins. The pronoun in "لَهُمْ" refers to the descendants of Adam, even though they have not been mentioned; the narrative as a whole, wherever it occurs in full, includes them. "Al-Ighwa'" means misguidance (al-idlal).

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, and al-A'raj read "المُخْلَصِينَ" with a fatha on the lam, meaning those whom You have made sincere (akhlaṣtahum) for Your worship and Your piety. The majority read it with a kasra on the lam, meaning those who sincerely held faith in You and in Your messengers.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿قالَ هَذا صِراطٌ عَلَيَّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ﴾, the speaker is God, may He be blessed and exalted. It is possible that this is conveyed through an intermediary. al-Dahhak, Humayd, al-Nakha'i, Abu Raja', Ibn Sirin, Qatada, Qays ibn 'Abbad, Mujahid, and others read "عَلِيٌّ مُسْتَقِيمٌ" (lofty and straight), from loftiness and exaltedness. According to this reading, the demonstrative "هَذا" refers to sincerity. When Iblis was excepted from those who were sincere, God said to him: "This sincerity is an elevated, straight path, which you, by your misleading, cannot reach its people." The majority of readers read "عَلَيَّ" with a shadda and a fatha on the yaʾ; according to this reading, the demonstrative "هَذا" refers to the division of people into deviators and sincere ones. When Iblis divided people into these two categories, God said to him: "This is a path leading to Me," i.e., this is a matter whose outcome is to Me, and the Arabs say, "Your way in this matter is upon so-and-so," meaning the consideration of your affair belongs to him. This is similar to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿إنَّ رَبَّكَ لَبِالمِرْصادِ﴾ [al-Fajr: 14] ("Indeed your Lord is ever watchful"). According to this reading, the verse is a statement that includes a threat.

Then He began to inform about the safety of His righteous servants from Iblis, and addressed him, saying that he has no proof over them and no power.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of His saying "My servants" is specific to the people of faith and piety, not the general creation. Accordingly, ﴿إلا مَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ﴾ is an exception from something other than the first clause. The meaning is: "But whoever follows you among the deviators has authority over them." If we take "servants" in a general sense, including the worshippers among people, since God did not grant Iblis any authority over anyone, then we consider the exception to be of a lesser quantity in terms of number, since the disbelievers have no measure. The first view is more correct. The purpose is only to avoid falling into the exception of the majority from the minority, although the jurists have permitted it. Abu al-Ma'ali said: it is not known in Arabic usage, and this verse is the best of what its permitters have cited as evidence.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

They have no proof from the verse according to what I have explained.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿وَإنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمَوْعِدُهُمْ﴾ means the place where they will gather. A "mawʿid" relates to both time and place, and sometimes the place is mentioned without specifying the time of the appointment. "Ajma'in" is an emphasis, and it carries the sense of a circumstantial (ḥāl). His saying ﴿لَها سَبْعَةُ أبْوابٍ﴾: it was said that the Fire in its entirety consists of seven layers (aṭbāq), the highest of which is Jahannam, then Laẓā, then al-Ḥuṭama, then al-Saʿir, then Saqar, then al-Jaḥīm, in which is Abu Jahl, then al-Hawiya; and that in each layer of it there is a gate. Thus, according to this view, the gates are some above others. In this verse, He referred to the Fire as a whole by Jahannam, since it is the most famous of its abodes and the first of them, and it is the place of the disobedient believers who do not dwell eternally in it; for this reason it was narrated that Jahannam will be destroyed and will decay. It was also said: the Fire consists of layers as we mentioned, but the seven gates are all in Jahannam on one level, and from each gate one descends to the layer to which it leads. I have abridged what the exegetes mentioned about the distances between the gates, about the air of the Fire, and about the manner of the condition, since these are numerous sayings most of which lack support; they fall within the realm of the permissible, and God's power is greater than these. May God protect us from His Fire and cover us with His mercy by His bounty.

As for His saying "juz'," the majority read it with a hamza. Ibn Shihab read it with a damma on the zay, and a group read "juzz" with a shadda on the zay without a hamza, which is the reading of Ibn al-Qa'qa'.

The Almighty and Majestic said:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs.﴾ ﴿Enter them in peace, secure.﴾ ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, upon couches facing one another.﴾ ﴿No fatigue will touch them therein, nor will they be removed from it.﴾ ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, mentioned what He has prepared for the people of Paradise after mentioning what He has prepared for the people of the Fire, so that the contrast would be manifest. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-'uyunin" (and springs) with a damma on the ʿayn, while Nubayh, al-Jarrah, Abu Waqid, and Ya'qub, in the narration of Ruways, read it with a kasra on the ʿayn, like "buyut" and "shuyukh."

The majority read "ud-khulūhā" (enter them) as an imperative, meaning: it will be said to them, "Enter them." Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, read "ukhdilūhā" (they will be made to enter) with the verb in the passive voice, with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the kha', and with a damma on the tanwin of "ʿuyūnin," transferring the vowel of the hamza onto it. "As-salām" here may mean safety (as-salāmah), and it may mean greeting (at-taḥiyyah). "Al-ghill" (resentment) is hatred. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse that He removes resentment from the hearts of the people of Paradise, but He did not mention a specific place for this. It has been reported in some hadith that this occurs on the Sirat, and it has been reported in others that it occurs at the gates of Paradise. In the wording of some of them, it is said that the resentment will remain at the gates of Paradise like the watering-places of camels.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is on the basis that Allah makes this a figurative image by a color He creates there and the like, and this is like the hadith of the slaughtering of death. It is also possible that it is extracted from the breasts, and for that there are dark pearls, so it will be like the camel's sheltered(?) ones. In some hadiths it has been reported that the removal of resentment occurs only after they have settled in Paradise. What is said about this is that Allah removes it at one place for some people and at another place for others. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I hope that I, Talhah, and az-Zubayr will be among those of whom Allah said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, upon couches facing one another.﴾" It is mentioned that a son of Talhah was with him, and al-Ashtar asked permission to enter, so he (ʿAli) detained him for a while, then permitted him, and he entered. He said: "Is this why you detained me? And likewise, if it were the son of ʿUthman, would you have detained him for him?" ʿAli said: "Yes. Indeed, I, ʿUthman, Talhah, and az-Zubayr are among those of whom Allah said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾, the verse." It has also been reported that the one seeking permission was other than al-Ashtar.

"Ikhwānan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). This is the brotherhood of religion and affection. "Akh" (brother) in this sense is pluralized as ikhwān and ikhwah, while "akh" in the sense of kinship is pluralized as ikhwah and ākhāʾ, and from it is the saying of the poet:

؎ And which of the sons of the ākhāʾ (kin) have their paths clear?

"As-surur" is the plural of sarīr (couch). As for "mutaqābilīn" (facing one another), the apparent meaning is: in the faces, since the couches face each other, and this is more beautiful in adornment. Mujahid said: "None of them looks at the back of his companion." It was also said: "facing one another in affection," and other things were said that the wording does not indicate.

"An-naṣab" is fatigue (at-taʿab), which applies to little and much. From the greater usage is the saying of Musa, upon him be peace: ﴿Indeed we have encountered in this journey of ours considerable fatigue﴾ [al-Kahf: 62], and from it is the saying of the poet:

؎ Leave me to a worry, O Umaymah, that tires.

His saying, exalted is He, "nabbi'" means: inform. "ʿIbādī" is the object of "nabbi'," and it transitively takes three objects, so "ʿibādī" is one object, and "anna" fills the place of the remaining two objects. This is agreed upon, and it and what it governs are in the position of a single noun. Do you not see that when you say: "It pleased me that Zayd is departing," the meaning is: "The departure of Zayd pleased me," because its entrance is only upon a nominal sentence of subject and predicate, so it fills the place of the two objects. "Nabba'a" may also take only two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Who informed you of this?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 3], and in this place it means: inform and make known. All of this is open to consideration.

This is a verse of hope and fear. It has been reported on this meaning from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "If the servant knew the extent of Allah's pardon, he would not refrain from what is forbidden; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would destroy himself." It has also been reported that the cause of this verse was that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to a group of his companions at the gate of Banu Shayba in the Haram and found them laughing, so he rebuked them and admonished them, then turned away. Jibril came to him from Allah and said: "O Muhammad, do you make My servants despair?" and recited the verse to him, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to them with it and informed them. Even if this were not the cause, what preceded it would require it, since the mention of what is in the Fire and what is in Paradise had already preceded, so Allah emphasized alerting people through this verse.

Allah, exalted is He, mentioned what He has prepared for the people of Paradise after mentioning what He has prepared for the people of the Fire, so that the contrast would be manifest. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "wa-'uyunin" (and springs) with a damma on the ʿayn, while Nubayh, al-Jarrah, Abu Waqid, and Ya'qub, in the narration of Ruways, read it with a kasra on the ʿayn, like "buyut" and "shuyukh."

The majority read "ud-khulūhā" (enter them) as an imperative, meaning: it will be said to them, "Enter them." Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, read "ukhdilūhā" (they will be made to enter) with the verb in the passive voice, with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the kha', and with a damma on the tanwin of "ʿuyūnin," transferring the vowel of the hamza onto it. "As-salām" here may mean safety (as-salāmah), and it may mean greeting (at-taḥiyyah). "Al-ghill" (resentment) is hatred. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse that He removes resentment from the hearts of the people of Paradise, but He did not mention a specific place for this. It has been reported in some hadith that this occurs on the Sirat, and it has been reported in others that it occurs at the gates of Paradise. In the wording of some of them, it is said that the resentment will remain at the gates of Paradise like the watering-places of camels.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is on the basis that Allah makes this a figurative image by a color He creates there and the like, and this is like the hadith of the slaughtering of death. It is also possible that it is extracted from the breasts, and for that there are dark pearls, so it will be like the camel's sheltered(?) ones. In some hadiths it has been reported that the removal of resentment occurs only after they have settled in Paradise. What is said about this is that Allah removes it at one place for some people and at another place for others. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I hope that I, Talhah, and az-Zubayr will be among those of whom Allah said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, upon couches facing one another.﴾" It is mentioned that a son of Talhah was with him, and al-Ashtar asked permission to enter, so he (ʿAli) detained him for a while, then permitted him, and he entered. He said: "Is this why you detained me? And likewise, if it were the son of ʿUthman, would you have detained him for him?" ʿAli said: "Yes. Indeed, I, ʿUthman, Talhah, and az-Zubayr are among those of whom Allah said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾, the verse." It has also been reported that the one seeking permission was other than al-Ashtar.

"Ikhwānan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). This is the brotherhood of religion and affection. "Akh" (brother) in this sense is pluralized as ikhwān and ikhwah, while "akh" in the sense of kinship is pluralized as ikhwah and ākhāʾ, and from it is the saying of the poet:

؎ And which of the sons of the ākhāʾ (kin) have their paths clear?

"As-surur" is the plural of sarīr (couch). As for "mutaqābilīn" (facing one another), the apparent meaning is: in the faces, since the couches face each other, and this is more beautiful in adornment. Mujahid said: "None of them looks at the back of his companion." It was also said: "facing one another in affection," and other things were said that the wording does not indicate.

"An-naṣab" is fatigue (at-taʿab), which applies to little and much. From the greater usage is the saying of Musa, upon him be peace: ﴿Indeed we have encountered in this journey of ours considerable fatigue﴾ [al-Kahf: 62], and from it is the saying of the poet:

؎ Leave me to a worry, O Umaymah, that tires.

His saying, exalted is He, "nabbi'" means: inform. "ʿIbādī" is the object of "nabbi'," and it transitively takes three objects, so "ʿibādī" is one object, and "anna" fills the place of the remaining two objects. This is agreed upon, and it and what it governs are in the position of a single noun. Do you not see that when you say: "It pleased me that Zayd is departing," the meaning is: "The departure of Zayd pleased me," because its entrance is only upon a nominal sentence of subject and predicate, so it fills the place of the two objects. "Nabba'a" may also take only two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Who informed you of this?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 3], and in this place it means: inform and make known. All of this is open to consideration.

This is a verse of hope and fear. It has been reported on this meaning from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "If the servant knew the extent of Allah's pardon, he would not refrain from what is forbidden; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would destroy himself." It has also been reported that the cause of this verse was that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to a group of his companions at the gate of Banu Shayba in the Haram and found them laughing, so he rebuked them and admonished them, then turned away. Jibril came to him from Allah and said: "O Muhammad, do you make My servants despair?" and recited the verse to him, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to them with it and informed them. Even if this were not the cause, what preceded it would require it, since the mention of what is in the Fire and what is in Paradise had already preceded, so Allah emphasized alerting people through this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 15, verses 51–56:

(p-298) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And inform them about the guests of Abraham﴾ ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you."﴾ ﴿They said, "Do not fear. Indeed, we give you good news of a boy who will be learned."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you give me good news although old age has touched me? Then by what do you give good news?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have given you good news in truth, so do not be of the despairing."﴾ ﴿He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?"﴾

Abu Haywa recited "wa-nabbihum" (with a ḍamma on the hā' and without hamza), and this is the start of a narrative after the first purpose has ended. "Al-ḍayf" (the guest) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) described by the word, so it is used for the singular, the dual, the plural, the masculine and the feminine with one form. An-Naḥḥās and others said: the estimate is "about the people of the guest" (ʿan aṣḥāb ḍayf).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What dispenses with this is that this maṣdar was treated as nouns are treated, as was done with "rahn" and similar words. What is meant by "al-ḍayf" here are the angels who came to destroy the people of Lot and gave good news to Abraham, peace be upon them both, and their story has already been mentioned.

His saying "salaman" is an accusative maṣdar governed by a hidden verb, whose estimate is: "We say peace" (sallamnā), or "We greet with a greeting" (nusallimu salāman). "Salām" here means greeting (taḥiyya). His saying "salaman" is a quotation of their words, so the verb "qāla" does not govern it; it governs only when what follows is a paraphrase of speech that is not quoted verbatim, as when you say to someone who said "There is no god but Allah": "You spoke the truth," and similar.

His saying ﴿Indeed, we are fearful of you﴾ means: frightened. Abraham, peace be upon him, felt fear of them when he set before them the roasted calf and saw that they did not eat; among them the sign of safety was eating food, and likewise it remains, throughout time, a security for the one who alights and the one who is alighted upon.

The majority read "tawjal" as the imperfect of "wajila." Al-Ḥasan read it with a ḍamma on the tā' in the passive of "awjala," because "wajila" is not transitive. This good news was of Isaac, and that was (p-299) some time after the birth of Ishmael. Abraham's saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, who gave me in old age Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [Ibrahim: 39] does not require that they were granted to him at that time; rather, it was much earlier than the praise.

The majority read "abashshartumūnī" with an interrogative alif, while al-Aʿraj read "bashartumūnī" without alif. His saying ﴿although old age has touched me﴾ means: in a state in which old age has touched me. Ibn Muḥayṣin read "al-kubr" with a ḍamma on the kāf and a sukūn on the bā'. Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read "tubashshirūn" with a fatḥa on the nūn which is the sign of the nominative; the verb, on this reading, is intransitive. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read "tubashshirūnnī" with a shaddated nūn and a yā'; Ibn Kathīr read with a shaddated nūn without yā', and in this reading the nūn of the sign was assimilated into the nūn of the first person, preparing for the yā'. Nāfiʿ read "tubashshirūnī" with a kasra on the nūn, and Abū Ḥātim considered Nāfiʿ's reading an error, saying that the poetic evidence for this is only a case of necessity (iḍṭirār).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an overreach on his part. The estimate of this reading is that the nūn of the first person was deleted, and the nūn which is the sign of the nominative was given a kasra to match the yā', then the yā' was deleted, the kasra indicating it. Similar to this is the saying of the poet, cited by Sībawayh:

﴿ tarāhu kaṯ-ṯaghāmi yuʿallu miskan ∗∗∗ yasurru l-fāliyyāti idhā falaynī ﴾

And among the deletion of this nūn is the saying of another poet:

﴿ abil-mawti lladhī lā budda annī ∗∗∗ ∗∗∗ mulāqin, lā abāki, tukhawwifīnī? ﴾

And from the deletion of this nūn is the saying of the poet:

﴿ qadnī min naṣr al-Khubaybayni qadī ﴾

He means ʿAbd Allah and Muṣʿab, the two sons of al-Zubayr, and ʿAbd Allah was called Abū Khubayb.

Al-Ḥasan read "fabima tabshurūn" with a fatḥa on the tā' and a ḍamma on the shīn.

Abraham's saying ﴿then by what do you give good news?﴾ is a confirmation in the manner of wonder and disbelief at their old age, or in the manner of belittling and indifference to joys because life has passed and old age has taken hold. Mujāhid said: he wondered at his own old age and at the old age of his wife; the mention of his age at the time of the good news has already been made.

Their saying ﴿We have given you good news in truth﴾ contains a certain emphasis, meaning: rejoice in what you have been given good news of, and leave aside anything else. The majority of people read "al-qāniṭīn" (the despairing). Despair (qunūṭ) is the complete form of hopelessness. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Muṣarrif, and it is narrated from ʿAmr: "al-qaniṭīn." Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamza read "wa-man yaqnaṭu" with a fatḥa on the nūn throughout the Qur'an. Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisā'ī read it with a kasra, and all of them read "min baʿdi mā qanaṭū" with a fatḥa on the nūn. Abū ʿUbayda rejected the reading of the people of the two Ḥaramayn and denied that one may say "qaniṭa" with a kasra on the nūn. It is not as he said, for they do not agree except upon what is strong in the language and is transmitted from them; it is a eloquent reading. One says "qanaṭa yaqnuṭu" and "qanita yaqnaṭu," like "naqama" and "naqima." Al-Aʿmash read here "yaqniṭu" with a kasra on the nūn, and he read "min baʿdi mā qanituū" also with a kasra on the nūn; thus he read in both dialects. Al-Ashhab read "yaqnuṭu" with a ḍamma on the nūn, which is the reading of al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash as well, and it is the dialect of Tamīm.
