What is meant by "al-ḍayf" here are the angels who came to destroy the people of Lot and gave good news to Abraham, peace be upon them both, and their story has already been mentioned.

His saying "salaman" is an accusative maṣdar governed by a hidden verb, whose estimate is: "We say peace" (sallamnā), or "We greet with a greeting" (nusallimu salāman). "Salām" here means greeting (taḥiyya). His saying "salaman" is a quotation of their words, so the verb "qāla" does not govern it; it governs only when what follows is a paraphrase of speech that is not quoted verbatim, as when you say to someone who said "There is no god but Allah": "You spoke the truth," and similar.

His saying ﴿Indeed, we are fearful of you﴾ means: frightened. Abraham, peace be upon him, felt fear of them when he set before them the roasted calf and saw that they did not eat; among them the sign of safety was eating food, and likewise it remains, throughout time, a security for the one who alights and the one who is alighted upon.

The majority read "tawjal" as the imperfect of "wajila." Al-Ḥasan read it with a ḍamma on the tā' in the passive of "awjala," because "wajila" is not transitive. This good news was of Isaac, and that was (p-299) some time after the birth of Ishmael. Abraham's saying ﴿Praise be to Allah, who gave me in old age Ishmael and Isaac﴾ [Ibrahim: 39] does not require that they were granted to him at that time; rather, it was much earlier than the praise.

The majority read "abashshartumūnī" with an interrogative alif, while al-Aʿraj read "bashartumūnī" without alif. His saying ﴿although old age has touched me﴾ means: in a state in which old age has touched me. Ibn Muḥayṣin read "al-kubr" with a ḍamma on the kāf and a sukūn on the bā'. Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read "tubashshirūn" with a fatḥa on the nūn which is the sign of the nominative; the verb, on this reading, is intransitive. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī read "tubashshirūnnī" with a shaddated nūn and a yā'; Ibn Kathīr read with a shaddated nūn without yā', and in this reading the nūn of the sign was assimilated into the nūn of the first person, preparing for the yā'. Nāfiʿ read "tubashshirūnī" with a kasra on the nūn, and Abū Ḥātim considered Nāfiʿ's reading an error, saying that the poetic evidence for this is only a case of necessity (iḍṭirār).

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an overreach on his part. The estimate of this reading is that the nūn of the first person was deleted, and the nūn which is the sign of the nominative was given a kasra to match the yā', then the yā' was deleted, the kasra indicating it. Similar to this is the saying of the poet, cited by Sībawayh:

﴿ tarāhu kaṯ-ṯaghāmi yuʿallu miskan ∗∗∗ yasurru l-fāliyyāti idhā falaynī ﴾

And among the deletion of this nūn is the saying of another poet:

﴿ abil-mawti lladhī lā budda annī ∗∗∗ ∗∗∗ mulāqin, lā abāki, tukhawwifīnī? ﴾

And from the deletion of this nūn is the saying of the poet:

﴿ qadnī min naṣr al-Khubaybayni qadī ﴾

He means ʿAbd Allah and Muṣʿab, the two sons of al-Zubayr, and ʿAbd Allah was called Abū Khubayb.

Al-Ḥasan read "fabima tabshurūn" with a fatḥa on the tā' and a ḍamma on the shīn.

Abraham's saying ﴿then by what do you give good news?﴾ is a confirmation in the manner of wonder and disbelief at their old age, or in the manner of belittling and indifference to joys because life has passed and old age has taken hold. Mujāhid said: he wondered at his own old age and at the old age of his wife; the mention of his age at the time of the good news has already been made.

Their saying ﴿We have given you good news in truth﴾ contains a certain emphasis, meaning: rejoice in what you have been given good news of, and leave aside anything else. The majority of people read "al-qāniṭīn" (the despairing). Despair (qunūṭ) is the complete form of hopelessness. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Muṣarrif, and it is narrated from ʿAmr: "al-qaniṭīn." Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamza read "wa-man yaqnaṭu" with a fatḥa on the nūn throughout the Qur'an. Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisā'ī read it with a kasra, and all of them read "min baʿdi mā qanaṭū" with a fatḥa on the nūn. Abū ʿUbayda rejected the reading of the people of the two Ḥaramayn and denied that one may say "qaniṭa" with a kasra on the nūn. It is not as he said, for they do not agree except upon what is strong in the language and is transmitted from them; it is a eloquent reading. One says "qanaṭa yaqnuṭu" and "qanita yaqnaṭu," like "naqama" and "naqima." Al-Aʿmash read here "yaqniṭu" with a kasra on the nūn, and he read "min baʿdi mā qanituū" also with a kasra on the nūn; thus he read in both dialects. Al-Ashhab read "yaqnuṭu" with a ḍamma on the nūn, which is the reading of al-Ḥasan and al-Aʿmash as well, and it is the dialect of Tamīm.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 15, verses 57–65:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿He said, "What is your business, O messengers?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We have been sent to a guilty people,﴾ ﴿except the family of Lot. Indeed, we will save them all,﴾ ﴿except his wife; We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿So when the messengers came to the family of Lot,﴾ ﴿he said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown to me."﴾ ﴿They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they used to dispute,﴾ ﴿and we have brought you the truth, and indeed we are truthful.﴾ ﴿So travel with your family during a portion of the night and follow behind them, and let none of you look back, and proceed where you are commanded."﴾

The speaker here is Abraham, peace be upon him. His words, "What is your business?", are a question containing a certain harshness, as when you say to someone whose condition you disapprove of, "What has befallen you? What is your calamity?", while you only intend to ask about his state. This is because the word *khatb* (business, matter) is used only for grave affairs. Moreover, the fact that they addressed him as "O messengers" and that they had given him good news suggests that he already knew they were angels when he said, "What is your business?" So his words, "What is your business?", may be understood, along with this, as attributing the *khatb* to them in so far as they were its bearers to the people who were to be punished. That is: what is this affair that you are carrying, and to which nation?

"The guilty people" refers to the people of the city of Sodom, to whom Lot, peace be upon him, was sent. The *mujrim* (guilty one) is the one who commits crimes and engages in what is forbidden. The root of *jaram* and *ajram* is "to earn." From this is the poet's saying:

> *Jarimat nahid fi ra's nik*
> (the earning of a bird of prey at the summit of a cliff)

That is, the earning of punishment on the peak of a lofty height. But the word, by custom, has been restricted to evil, so one does not call someone who earns reward a *mujrim*.

Their words, *illa al* ("except the family of"), constitute a disconnected exception (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning an exception that does not fall under the same category as what precedes it. *Al* means the people whose affair returns to the one they are attributed to. So Sibawayh said. This is explicit evidence that the word *al* is not the word *ahl* (family), as al-Nahhas said. On this basis it is permissible to attach *al* to a pronoun. As for *uhayl*, it is the diminutive of *ahl*, and they used it to avoid the diminutive of *al*, so they rejected *uwayl*.

The majority of the Seven readers recited *lamunajjuhum* (with doubled *jim*). Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited it with the lightened form. The pronoun in *munajjuhum* is in the genitive position through the attachment, and the nun was dropped for the sake of the substitution (*mu'aqaba*). This is the view of the majority of the grammarians. Al-Akhfash said: the pronoun is in the accusative position, and the nun was dropped because it is necessary for this pronoun to be attached.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Here there is room for consideration.

His words, Exalted is He, *illa imra'atahu* ("except his wife"), are an exception after an exception. Both are disconnected exceptions, as some grammarians have related, because they did not count his unbelieving wife among his family.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

There is room for consideration in this, because before the exception she is included in the term *al*, which is the family. It is not so with *al* alongside the guilty. So the first exception appears to be disconnected and the second connected. An exception after an exception returns the second excepted item to the ruling of the first matter. Some people gave the example of your saying: "I have one hundred dirhams except ten dirhams except two dirhams," so the two dirhams fall under the ruling of the ninety dirhams. Al-Mubarrad said: this example is not good, because it is the invention of speech and its rejection, since there is a way to express the meaning more beautifully than this convoluted construction, namely to say: "I have a hundred except eight." What should serve as an example for the verse is your saying: "I struck the Banu Tamim except the Banu Darim except a chamberlain (*hajib*)," because the *hajib* is one of the Banu Darim. Since the first excepted item contains within it what the ruling does not apply to, and necessity brings it into its wording, and we cannot express it without that which the ruling does not apply to, we are compelled to use a second exception.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Al-Mubarrad's inclination in this is noble.

All of them, except 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, recited *qaddarna* with a doubled *dal* throughout the Qur'an. 'Asim recited it with a lightened *dal*, and in the transmission of Hafs it is with the heavy form. The lightened form can have the meaning of the heavy form, as the Hudhali poet Abu Dhu'ayb said:

> *Wa mufrihatin 'ansin qadartu li-saqiha*
> *fakharrat kama tatabi'u al-rihu bi-al-qufl*
>
> (And a she-camel, swift and strong, I measured out [my blow] at her shank, so she fell as the wind follows the grassy cliffs [in rapid succession].)

He means: I aimed my striking at her shank. Also like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the prayer of istikhara: "And decree for me the good wherever it may be." It can also mean "make easy and grant success," and from this is the poet's saying:

> *Bi-Qandahar wa man tuqdar maniyyatuhu*
> *bi-Qandahar yurajjam dunahu al-khabar*
>
> (In Qandahar, and whoever his death is decreed for, in Qandahar, news is stoned before reaching him.)

The alif in *innaha* is pronounced with a kasra because of the lam in His words, Exalted is He, *lamina* ("among"). *Al-ghabir* is that which remains, in time or otherwise. A group, among them al-Nahhas, said: it is among the *adda* (words having contrary meanings), used both for what has passed and for what remains. But in this verse it means remaining, that is: among those who remain behind in the punishment.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So when the messengers came to the family of Lot﴾ and what follows. The discourse and the narration of the stories concerning Lot have preceded, as has the manner of the messengers' meeting with him. It has been said that the messengers were three: Gabriel, Michael and Israfil. It has also been said that they were twelve. His words, "*munkarun*" (unknown), mean: you are not known in this region. In this word there is a warning, and it belongs to the pattern of his censure of his people, and his tendency to avoid lodging these people in that city, out of fear that the evil of their deeds and their pursuit of abominations would become apparent. The messengers then said to Lot: "Rather, we have brought you what God promised you of their punishment for their disbelief and their sins, which is what they used to doubt and did not verify."

A group recited *fa-asri* with a connected alif, and a group with a cut alif. It is said *sara* and *asra* with the same meaning, when one travels by night. The poet al-Nabigha said:

> *Asrat 'alayhi min al-Jawza'i sariyatun*
>
> (A traveling [star] of Orion's [season] traveled by night over him.)

Thus he combined both dialects. Al-Yamani recited *fa-sir bi-ahlika* ("so travel with your family"). This command to travel by night comes from God, Exalted is He; that is, it is said to you. *Al-qit'* is a portion of the night. A group recited *biqita'in* with a fatha on the *ta'*, as related by Mundhir ibn Sa'id.

His words, ﴿and follow behind them﴾, mean: be behind them and at their rear, until none of them remains and no one turns back. *Haythu* in its well-known usage is a locative adverb. A group said: Lot was commanded to travel toward Zughar. It has also been said: to a place of safety not known to us. A group said: *haythu* may also be a temporal adverb, and Abu 'Ali cited in this the verse of Tarafa:

> *Li-al-fata 'aqlun ya'ishu bihi*
> *haythu tahdi sakahu qadamuhu*
>
> (The young man has an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot guides his leg.)

As if he said: for the duration of his walking and his movement. This verse, in that He commanded him to travel with a portion of the night, and then said to him "wherever you are commanded," we find in the verse no command to him except in His words ﴿with a portion of the night﴾, so it is possible that *haythu* is a temporal adverb.

*Yaltafit* is derived from *iltifat*, which is the turning of the eye. Mujahid said: the meaning is: let none of you look behind him. They were forbidden to look, out of fear of heedlessness and of the soul's attachment to those left behind. It has also been said: rather, so that their hearts would not break from witnessing what befell the town in its uplifting and overturning. It has also been said: *yaltafit* means *yalwi* (turn aside), from your saying *laftu al-amr* when you twisted it, and from this is their saying of a poem: *lafita*, because some of its parts are twisted upon others.

Here there is room for consideration.

> (In Qandahar, and whoever his death is decreed for, in Qandahar, news is stoned before reaching him.)

The alif in *innaha* is pronounced with a kasra because of the lam in His words, Exalted is He, *lamina* ("among"). *Al-ghabir* is that which remains, in time or otherwise. A group, among them al-Nahhas, said: it is among the *adda* (words having contrary meanings), used both for what has passed and for what remains. But in this verse it means remaining, that is: among those who remain behind in the punishment.

His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So when the messengers came to the family of Lot﴾ and what follows. The discourse and the narration of the stories concerning Lot have preceded, as has the manner of the messengers' meeting with him. It has been said that the messengers were three: Gabriel, Michael and Israfil. It has also been said that they were twelve. His words, "*munkarun*" (unknown), mean: you are not known in this region. In this word there is a warning, and it belongs to the pattern of his censure of his people, and his tendency to avoid lodging these people in that city, out of fear that the evil of their deeds and their pursuit of abominations would become apparent. The messengers then said to Lot: "Rather, we have brought you what God promised you of their punishment for their disbelief and their sins, which is what they used to doubt and did not verify."

A group recited *fa-asri* with a connected alif, and a group with a cut alif. It is said *sara* and *asra* with the same meaning, when one travels by night. The poet al-Nabigha said:

> *Asrat 'alayhi min al-Jawza'i sariyatun*
>
> (A traveling [star] of Orion's [season] traveled by night over him.)

Thus he combined both dialects. Al-Yamani recited *fa-sir bi-ahlika* ("so travel with your family"). This command to travel by night comes from God, Exalted is He; that is, it is said to you. *Al-qit'* is a portion of the night. A group recited *biqita'in* with a fatha on the *ta'*, as related by Mundhir ibn Sa'id.

His words, ﴿and follow behind them﴾, mean: be behind them and at their rear, until none of them remains and no one turns back. *Haythu* in its well-known usage is a locative adverb. A group said: Lot was commanded to travel toward Zughar. It has also been said: to a place of safety not known to us. A group said: *haythu* may also be a temporal adverb, and Abu 'Ali cited in this the verse of Tarafa:

> *Li-al-fata 'aqlun ya'ishu bihi*
> *haythu tahdi sakahu qadamuhu*
>
> (The young man has an intellect by which he lives, wherever his foot guides his leg.)

As if he said: for the duration of his walking and his movement. This verse, in that He commanded him to travel with a portion of the night, and then said to him "wherever you are commanded," we find in the verse no command to him except in His words ﴿with a portion of the night﴾, so it is possible that *haythu* is a temporal adverb.

*Yaltafit* is derived from *iltifat*, which is the turning of the eye. Mujahid said: the meaning is: let none of you look behind him. They were forbidden to look, out of fear of heedlessness and of the soul's attachment to those left behind. It has also been said: rather, so that their hearts would not break from witnessing what befell the town in its uplifting and overturning. It has also been said: *yaltafit* means *yalwi* (turn aside), from your saying *laftu al-amr* when you twisted it, and from this is their saying of a poem: *lafita*, because some of its parts are twisted upon others.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 15, verses 66–77:**

The Most High said:

﴿And We decreed that matter to him: that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning.﴾ ﴿And the people of the city came, rejoicing.﴾ ﴿He said: "These are my guests, so do not disgrace me.﴾ ﴿And fear God and do not humiliate me."﴾ ﴿They said: "Did we not forbid you from [receiving] the people of the worlds?"﴾ ﴿He said: "These are my daughters, if you are going to act."﴾ ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication.﴾ ﴿So the Cry seized them at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And We turned it upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾

**The meaning:** "And We decreed that matter," i.e., We carried it out and made it certain. Then He placed "to him" into the speech, since it was revealed to him and God informed him of it. Thus this meaning is conveyed concisely, and what the apparent wording indicates has been omitted. The word "that" (anna) is in the accusative position. Al-Akhfash said it is an apposition (badal) for "that" (dhalika), while al-Farra' said the sense is "bi-anna dabira" ("that the remnant of"), with the preposition omitted. The first view is more correct.

"Dabir" is the one who comes at the end of a people, i.e., at their rear. When that is cut off and it reaches the last of them, the punishment has come upon them from first to last. These expressions denote total extermination and complete destruction. It is said: "God cut off his dabir," "he uprooted his sha'fa," and "he silenced his na'ma," all with the same meaning. "Musbihin" means: when they enter the morning and reach daybreak.

The Most High's words, ﴿And the people of the city came, rejoicing﴾, may refer to a matter that occurred before Lut was informed of the destruction of his people. This is supported by the fact that Lut's argument with his people implies that those who did not know of their destruction were weak, and that the guests were angels. It is also possible that His words ﴿And the people of the city came﴾ refer to the time after he knew of their destruction, and that what they said in the exchange that follows was in the manner of mockery toward him, giving him respite, and waiting for him.

Abu Muhammad the Judge, may God have mercy on him, said:

The first possibility is more likely in my view, and it is the apparent meaning from verses in other surahs. His words "rejoicing" mean: at the guests, out of their hope for indecency. "Dayf" (guest) is a verbal noun that has been described by this form, so it applies to the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine.

As for their words ﴿Did we not forbid you from [receiving] the people of the worlds?﴾: it is related that they had previously warned him not to host anyone or to give anyone protection, because they did not respect him and did not refrain from seeking indecency from the guests. Al-A'mash read "Inna dabira" with a kasra on the hamza. It is also related that in the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it is: "And We decreed that matter to him, and We said: indeed the remnant of these...". Al-Suddi mentioned that they only committed indecency with strangers, and did not commit it among themselves; so they would waylay the roads.

As for Lut's words, peace be upon him, ﴿These are my daughters﴾, scholars differed about their interpretation. It was said that he meant the women of his community, because the wives of the prophets are the mothers of their communities, and he is their father; so the women are his "daughters" in terms of sanctity. The intended meaning is marriage. This interpretation entails that in his law it was permissible for a disbeliever to marry a believing woman, though it is reported that believers among them were very few. It was also said that he meant only his biological daughters, and that he called them to marriage as well; this is the view of Qatada. This interpretation also entails what was entailed for the previous view in our ordering. It is possible that by his words ﴿These are my daughters﴾, peace be upon him, he meant his biological daughters, and that this is in the manner of metaphor (majaz), and that it does not establish the permissibility of his daughters. This is like when you say to a person whom you see wanting to kill another: "Kill me and do not kill him." That is only in the manner of condemning him, pulling him down from some position, and summoning his shame. All of this is part of the exaggeration of speech which does not involve falsehood; rather its purpose is understood. Upon this is the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: "...even if it were like the nest of a sandgrouse." And other examples besides this.

"Al-'amr" and "al-'umr" with a fatha or damma on the 'ayn are the same: both mean the lifespan of life and its duration. It is used in oaths only with the fatha. In this verse there is honour for Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, because God the Most High swore by his life, and He did not do that with any human other than him. This is what Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said. The oath "by your life" (la-'amruka) in the Qur'an, and "by my life" (la-'amri) and similar expressions in Arabic poetry and eloquent speech, occurs in many places, as in his saying:

*By my life, and what is my life to me, is not easy.*

And another's saying:

*By the life of your father, Mu'alla was not disowned.*

And another's saying:

*By your life, indeed death has not missed the youth,*
*like the hanging long rope and its loops in the hand.*

The Arabs say "la-'amru Allah" (by the life of God), and from it is the poet's saying:

*When the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me,*
*by the life of God, their pleasure pleases me.*

Al-A'sha said:

*And by the life of him who made the months a sign among us,*
*so he made clear their half and their completion.*

Some scholars of meanings said: this is not permitted, because one does not say of God the Most High that He has a lifespan; rather one says "eternal subsistence." This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i disliked that a man say "la-'amri" (by my life), because he is swearing by the life of himself, and that is the speech of weak men, and similar. Malik's view regarding "la-'amri wa la-'amruka" (by my life and by your life) is that they are not oaths. Ibn Habib said that "la-'amruka" in speech should be used following this verse.

"Ya'mahun" means they become confused and bewildered. The pronouns in "their intoxication" refer to the people of Lut who were mentioned. Al-Tabari mentioned that the intended people were the Quraysh, but this is far-fetched, because it would break the connection with what comes before and after it. The phrase "in their intoxication" is metaphor and figurative comparison, meaning: in their misguidance, their heedlessness of the truth, and their frivolity. "Ya'mahun" means: they hesitate in their bewilderment. "Mushriqin" means: they had entered into the sunrise, which is the spreading and appearance of the sun's light; so said Ibn Zayd. This Cry is the cry of the destroying blast, and it was not like the cry of Thamud. They were destroyed after dawn, "musbihin," and the destruction completed them at sunrise, "mushriqin." The predicate of his words "By your life" is omitted, and its estimated form is: "By your life, my oath" or "my swearing." But there is something to be considered in this. Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-'amruka." Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read "la-fi sukratihim" with a damma on the sin. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "sakaratihim." Al-A'mash read "la-fi sukrihim" without a ta'. Abu 'Amr, in the narration of al-Jahdami, read "annahum" with a fatha on the hamza, "fi sakratihim."

It is related regarding the meaning of His words ﴿And We turned it upside down﴾ that Gabriel, peace be upon him, uprooted the city with his wing and lifted it until the angels of the heaven heard the crowing of roosters and the barking of dogs. Then he overturned it and let it all fall. Whoever had some of the rubble of the city fall upon him died, and whoever escaped from them was struck by stones of "sijjil." "Sijjil" is a name of one of the names of the lowest heaven. It was also said that it is a Persian word, referring to stones baked from clay like bricks and similar. This matter has already been discussed.

"Al-mutawassimun" (those who discern): Mujahid said: those who examine physiognomy; al-Dahhak said: those who look; Qatada said: those who take warning. Other things close to these have been said. All of this is an interpretation of its meaning, not of its wording. The meanings that exist in a person or other things, whether good or bad, show a mark (wasm) of those meanings upon them, such as tranquillity, piety, and the awe that comes from goodness, and similar. So the one who discerns (mutawassim) is the one who looks at the mark of a meaning in order to infer the meaning from it. It seems that the disobedience of these people left a mark of punishment and destruction, so whoever sees the mark infers disobedience from it, and his looking leads him to avoid sins, lest what befell them befall him. Among the poetry on this word is the poet's saying:

*I discerned him when I saw awe upon him,*
*and I said: this man is of the family of Hashim.*

Another said:

*And I remained standing among them, discerning.*

Another said:

*Indeed I discerned in you goodness as a supererogation.*

The pronoun in His words "And indeed it" may refer to the destroyed city, meaning: it is on a road visible to the one who takes warning. This is the interpretation of Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd. It may refer to the signs, or it may refer to the stones. This last interpretation is strengthened by what is related: that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Indeed the stones of punishment have been suspended between heaven and earth for two thousand years for the sinners of my community." His words "a sign" (la-ayah) mean an indicator and a marker, as when you say: "There is a sign between me and you, such and such."

*When the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me,*
*by the life of God, their pleasure pleases me.*

*And by the life of him who made the months a sign among us,*

Ibrahim al-Nakha'i disliked that a man say "la-'amri" (by my life), because he is swearing by the life of himself, and that is the speech of weak men, and similar. Malik's view regarding "la-'amri wa la-'amruka" (by my life and by your life) is that they are not oaths. Ibn Habib said that "la-'amruka" in speech should be used following this verse.

It is related regarding the meaning of His words ﴿And We turned it upside down﴾ that Gabriel, peace be upon him, uprooted the city with his wing and lifted it until the angels of the heaven heard the crowing of roosters and the barking of dogs. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 15, verses 66–77:**

The Most High said:

﴿And We decreed that matter to him: that the last remnant of these would be cut off by morning.﴾ ﴿And the people of the city came, rejoicing.﴾ ﴿He said: "These are my guests, so do not disgrace me.﴾ ﴿And fear God and do not humiliate me."﴾ ﴿They said: "Did we not forbid you from [receiving] the people of the worlds?"﴾ ﴿He said: "These are my daughters, if you are going to act."﴾ ﴿By your life, they were wandering blindly in their intoxication.﴾ ﴿So the Cry seized them at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And We turned it upside down and rained upon them stones of baked clay.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers.﴾

**The meaning:** "And We decreed that matter," i.e., We carried it out and made it certain. Then He placed "to him" into the speech, since it was revealed to him and God informed him of it. Thus this meaning is conveyed concisely, and what the apparent wording indicates has been omitted. The word "that" (anna) is in the accusative position. Al-Akhfash said it is an apposition (badal) for "that" (dhalika), while al-Farra' said the sense is "bi-anna dabira" ("that the remnant of"), with the preposition omitted. The first view is more correct.

"Dabir" is the one who comes at the end of a people, i.e., at their rear. When that is cut off and it reaches the last of them, the punishment has come upon them from first to last. These expressions denote total extermination and complete destruction. It is said: "God cut off his dabir," "he uprooted his sha'fa," and "he silenced his na'ma," all with the same meaning. "Musbihin" means: when they enter the morning and reach daybreak.

The Most High's words, ﴿And the people of the city came, rejoicing﴾, may refer to a matter that occurred before Lut was informed of the destruction of his people. This is supported by the fact that Lut's argument with his people implies that those who did not know of their destruction were weak, and that the guests were angels. It is also possible that His words ﴿And the people of the city came﴾ refer to the time after he knew of their destruction, and that what they said in the exchange that follows was in the manner of mockery toward him, giving him respite, and waiting for him.

Abu Muhammad the Judge, may God have mercy on him, said:

The first possibility is more likely in my view, and it is the apparent meaning from verses in other surahs. His words "rejoicing" mean: at the guests, out of their hope for indecency. "Dayf" (guest) is a verbal noun that has been described by this form, so it applies to the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine.

As for their words ﴿Did we not forbid you from [receiving] the people of the worlds?﴾: it is related that they had previously warned him not to host anyone or to give anyone protection, because they did not respect him and did not refrain from seeking indecency from the guests. Al-A'mash read "Inna dabira" with a kasra on the hamza. It is also related that in the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it is: "And We decreed that matter to him, and We said: indeed the remnant of these...". Al-Suddi mentioned that they only committed indecency with strangers, and did not commit it among themselves; so they would waylay the roads.

As for Lut's words, peace be upon him, ﴿These are my daughters﴾, scholars differed about their interpretation. It was said that he meant the women of his community, because the wives of the prophets are the mothers of their communities, and he is their father; so the women are his "daughters" in terms of sanctity. The intended meaning is marriage. This interpretation entails that in his law it was permissible for a disbeliever to marry a believing woman, though it is reported that believers among them were very few. It was also said that he meant only his biological daughters, and that he called them to marriage as well; this is the view of Qatada. This interpretation also entails what was entailed for the previous view in our ordering. It is possible that by his words ﴿These are my daughters﴾, peace be upon him, he meant his biological daughters, and that this is in the manner of metaphor (majaz), and that it does not establish the permissibility of his daughters. The first view is more correct.

"Dabir" is the one who comes at the end of a people, i.e., at their rear. When that is cut off and it reaches the last of them, the punishment has come upon them from first to last. These expressions denote total extermination and complete destruction. It is said: "God cut off his dabir," "he uprooted his sha'fa," and "he silenced his na'ma," all with the same meaning. "Musbihin" means: when they enter the morning and reach daybreak.

The Most High's words, ﴿And the people of the city came, rejoicing﴾, may refer to a matter that occurred before Lut was informed of the destruction of his people. This is supported by the fact that Lut's argument with his people implies that those who did not know of their destruction were weak, and that the guests were angels. It is also possible that His words ﴿And the people of the city came﴾ refer to the time after he knew of their destruction, and that what they said in the exchange that follows was in the manner of mockery toward him, giving him respite, and waiting for him.

Abu Muhammad the Judge, may God have mercy on him, said:

The first possibility is more likely in my view, and it is the apparent meaning from verses in other surahs. His words "rejoicing" mean: at the guests, out of their hope for indecency. "Dayf" (guest) is a verbal noun that has been described by this form, so it applies to the singular and the plural, the masculine and the feminine.

As for their words ﴿Did we not forbid you from [receiving] the people of the worlds?﴾: it is related that they had previously warned him not to host anyone or to give anyone protection, because they did not respect him and did not refrain from seeking indecency from the guests. Al-A'mash read "Inna dabira" with a kasra on the hamza. It is also related that in the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it is: "And We decreed that matter to him, and We said: indeed the remnant of these...". Al-Suddi mentioned that they only committed indecency with strangers, and did not commit it among themselves; so they would waylay the roads.

As for Lut's words, peace be upon him, ﴿These are my daughters﴾, scholars differed about their interpretation. It was said that he meant the women of his community, because the wives of the prophets are the mothers of their communities, and he is their father; so the women are his "daughters" in terms of sanctity. The intended meaning is marriage. This interpretation entails that in his law it was permissible for a disbeliever to marry a believing woman, though it is reported that believers among them were very few. It was also said that he meant only his biological daughters, and that he called them to marriage as well; this is the view of Qatada. This interpretation also entails what was entailed for the previous view in our ordering. It is possible that by his words ﴿These are my daughters﴾, peace be upon him, he meant his biological daughters, and that this is in the manner of metaphor (majaz), and that it does not establish the permissibility of his daughters. This is like when you say to a person whom you see wanting to kill another: "Kill me and do not kill him." That is only in the manner of condemning him, pulling him down from some position, and summoning his shame. All of this is part of the exaggeration of speech which does not involve falsehood; rather its purpose is understood. Upon this is the saying of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: "...even if it were like the nest of a sandgrouse." And other examples besides this.

"Al-'amr" and "al-'umr" with a fatha or damma on the 'ayn are the same: both mean the lifespan of life and its duration. It is used in oaths only with the fatha. In this verse there is honour for Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, because God the Most High swore by his life, and He did not do that with any human other than him. This is what Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said. The oath "by your life" (la-'amruka) in the Qur'an, and "by my life" (la-'amri) and similar expressions in Arabic poetry and eloquent speech, occurs in many places, as in his saying:

*By my life, and what is my life to me, is not easy.*

And another's saying:

*By the life of your father, Mu'alla was not disowned.*

And another's saying:

*By your life, indeed death has not missed the youth,*
*like the hanging long rope and its loops in the hand.*

The Arabs say "la-'amru Allah" (by the life of God), and from it is the poet's saying:

*When the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me,*
*by the life of God, their pleasure pleases me.*

Al-A'sha said:

*And by the life of him who made the months a sign among us,*
*so he made clear their half and their completion.*

Some scholars of meanings said: this is not permitted, because one does not say of God the Most High that He has a lifespan; rather one says "eternal subsistence." This was mentioned by al-Zahrawi. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i disliked that a man say "la-'amri" (by my life), because he is swearing by the life of himself, and that is the speech of weak men, and similar. Malik's view regarding "la-'amri wa la-'amruka" (by my life and by your life) is that they are not oaths. Ibn Habib said that "la-'amruka" in speech should be used following this verse.

"Ya'mahun" means they become confused and bewildered. The pronouns in "their intoxication" refer to the people of Lut who were mentioned. Al-Tabari mentioned that the intended people were the Quraysh, but this is far-fetched, because it would break the connection with what comes before and after it. The phrase "in their intoxication" is metaphor and figurative comparison, meaning: in their misguidance, their heedlessness of the truth, and their frivolity. "Ya'mahun" means: they hesitate in their bewilderment. "Mushriqin" means: they had entered into the sunrise, which is the spreading and appearance of the sun's light; so said Ibn Zayd. This Cry is the cry of the destroying blast, and it was not like the cry of Thamud. They were destroyed after dawn, "musbihin," and the destruction completed them at sunrise, "mushriqin." The predicate of his words "By your life" is omitted, and its estimated form is: "By your life, my oath" or "my swearing." But there is something to be considered in this. Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-'amruka." Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read "la-fi sukratihim" with a damma on the sin. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "sakaratihim." Al-A'mash read "la-fi sukrihim" without a ta'. Abu 'Amr, in the narration of al-Jahdami, read "annahum" with a fatha on the hamza, "fi sakratihim."

It is related regarding the meaning of His words ﴿And We turned it upside down﴾ that Gabriel, peace be upon him, uprooted the city with his wing and lifted it until the angels of the heaven heard the crowing of roosters and the barking of dogs. Then he overturned it and let it all fall. Whoever had some of the rubble of the city fall upon him died, and whoever escaped from them was struck by stones of "sijjil." "Sijjil" is a name of one of the names of the lowest heaven. It was also said that it is a Persian word, referring to stones baked from clay like bricks and similar. This matter has already been discussed.

"Al-mutawassimun" (those who discern): Mujahid said: those who examine physiognomy; al-Dahhak said: those who look; Qatada said: those who take warning. Other things close to these have been said. All of this is an interpretation of its meaning, not of its wording. The meanings that exist in a person or other things, whether good or bad, show a mark (wasm) of those meanings upon them, such as tranquillity, piety, and the awe that comes from goodness, and similar. So the one who discerns (mutawassim) is the one who looks at the mark of a meaning in order to infer the meaning from it. It seems that the disobedience of these people left a mark of punishment and destruction, so whoever sees the mark infers disobedience from it, and his looking leads him to avoid sins, lest what befell them befall him. Among the poetry on this word is the poet's saying:

*I discerned him when I saw awe upon him,*
*and I said: this man is of the family of Hashim.*

Another said:

*And I remained standing among them, discerning.*

Another said:

*Indeed I discerned in you goodness as a supererogation.*

The pronoun in His words "And indeed it" may refer to the destroyed city, meaning: it is on a road visible to the one who takes warning. This is the interpretation of Mujahid, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd. It may refer to the signs, or it may refer to the stones. This last interpretation is strengthened by what is related: that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Indeed the stones of punishment have been suspended between heaven and earth for two thousand years for the sinners of my community." His words "a sign" (la-ayah) mean an indicator and a marker, as when you say: "There is a sign between me and you, such and such."

(p. 312) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And indeed, the companions of the Thicket were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿So We took revenge upon them, and indeed they both are on a clear highway.﴾ ﴿And the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿And We gave them Our signs, but they were turning away from them.﴾ ﴿And they used to carve houses out of the mountains, secure.﴾ ﴿So the Shriek seized them at morning.﴾ ﴿And what they used to earn did not avail them.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth. And indeed, the Hour is coming, so forgive with gracious forgiveness.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Creator, the All-Knowing.﴾

"Al-Ayka" (al-ayka, the thicket): a dense, green cluster of trees, such as lote-trees and the like. Qatada said: It has been reported that the thicket of these people was of dum-palm trees. It was also said: of the muql tree, and it was said: of lote-trees. These people were a folk who dwelt in a thicket and benefited from it for their livelihoods. So God sent Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to them, and they disbelieved. God then imposed heat upon them, and it lasted over them for seven days. Then they saw a cloud, so they went out and sheltered beneath it, and it blazed into fire over them.

al-Tabari related: Shu'ayb was sent to two nations that disbelieved, and they were punished with two different punishments. The people of Madyan were punished with the Shriek, and the companions of the Thicket were punished with the canopy (al-zulla). The readers did not differ in this place regarding the insertion of the alif and lam on "ayka." Most of them hamzated the alif of "ayka" after the lam. It was reported from some of them that he eased it and transferred its vowel to the lam, reading "al-ayka" without hamza. They differed regarding it in Surat al-Shu'ara' and in Surat Sad.

"Inna" here is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy (thaqila), according to the school of the Basrans. Al-Farra' said: "in" means "ma" (not), and the lam in His saying "la-zalimin" means "illa" (except). Abu 'Ali said: "al-Ayk" is the plural of "ayka," like "tamra" and "tamr." Among the evidence for the word is the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

Like the weeping of doves over the branches
of the thicket, among the birds with lamenting cries.

(p. 313) And the verse of Jarir:

I stood there, and longing stirred in me,
while the doves of the thicket cooed to her in pairs.

And another's saying:

Behold, the world is but the freshness of a thicket:
when one side of it turns green, the other side dries up.

And the saying of al-Hudhali:

Adorned with two braids, close to her
is a cluster of the thicket, its short branches hanging over it.

And al-Asma'i recited:

And no deep-curved valley ... that casts onto the ground
the wood of the ayk and the dhall (tamarisk).

(p. 314) The pronoun in His saying "wa-innahuma" may refer to the two cities previously mentioned: the city of the people of Lot and the city of the companions of the Thicket. It may also refer to the two prophets, Lot and Shu'ayb, in that they are both upon a path from God and a clear law.

"Al-imam" in the speech of the Arabs is that which is followed and taken as a guide. They say it of the line used for building. It may be the road, it may be a clear book, it may be the measure by which craftsmen work, and it may be a man who is followed as an example, and the like. Whoever holds that the pronoun in "innahuma" returns to the two cities says: "al-imam" is the road. It was also said, on that basis: "al-imam" is the Book in which their destruction was predestined.

"Ashab al-Hijr" are Thamud, whose story has already been mentioned. "Al-Hijr" is their city, which lies between Medina and Tabuk. He said "al-mursalin" (the messengers) because whoever denies one messenger is required to deny all of them, since the matter of belief is one for all the messengers together. Thus this expression is more severe upon the deniers.

The signs that God gave them were the she-camel and what it contained of breaking the customary course, as its explanation and expansion were previously mentioned. Abu Haywa read "wa-atayna-hum ayatana" in the singular.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they used to carve﴾ (the verse). It describes the people of Salih with intense attention to this world and to seeking gain from it. He mentioned as an example that they used to carve their houses in the rocky mountains. "Al-nahт" (carving) is hewing with picks and the like out of stone or wood and the like. The majority of people read "yanhituna" with a kasra on the ha'. Al-Hasan read it with a fatha, and this is because of the throat letter (harf al-halq), and this is the reading of Abu Haywa. As for His saying "amin" (secure), it was said: its meaning is: safe from their collapse. It was said: safe from the calamities of this world. It was said: safe from death, due to their delusion through the length of their hopes.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak, and the most evident opinion regarding it is that they felt secure from the consequences of the Hereafter, (p. 315) so they did not act according to what it required, but rather acted according to the security they felt from it.

The meaning of "musbihin" is: upon their entering the morning. It is mentioned that this was a Saturday. The story of their punishment, their appointed time, and the changing of their colors has already been mentioned. The intensity of their attention to this world and their seeking of gain did not avail them anything, nor did it ward off the punishment of God.

The first "ma" is for negation, and it may also be interrogative of affirmation (taqrir); the second is verbal (masdariyya).

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth﴾ (the verse). The intended meaning is that these people who strive for this world, whom their striving did not avail, are of no account. The heavens and the earth and all things were not created in vain, nor left aimless, nor so that they might be an act of obedience to God as these people and their likes did. Rather, they were created with truth, for a necessary and intended purpose and for aims that have ends of punishment and bliss. And indeed the Hour is coming upon all the affairs of this world. That is: so do not grieve, O Muhammad, over the deeds of your people, for the recompense is waiting for them in ambush. So forgive their deeds, that is: turn away from them by withdrawing from them. He emphasized the forgiveness with the description of gracefulness (al-jamal), since what is meant by it is that there should be no reproach in it and no reproach-making. This verse implies a truce, and it was abrogated (nasakha, naskh) by the verse of the sword, as Qatada said.

Then He consoled him at the end of the verse by stating that God, exalted is He, creates whom He wills for whom He wills, and He, exalted is He, knows the wisdom in that, not these idols that you worship. The majority of people read "al-Khallaq" (the Creator), and al-A'mash and al-Jahdari read "al-Khaliq."

Rather, they were created with truth, for a necessary and intended purpose and for aims that have ends of punishment and bliss. And indeed the Hour is coming upon all the affairs of this world. The majority of people read "al-Khallaq" (the Creator), and al-A'mash and al-Jahdari read "al-Khaliq."

(p. 312) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And indeed, the companions of the Thicket were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿So We took revenge upon them, and indeed they both are on a clear highway.﴾ ﴿And the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿And We gave them Our signs, but they were turning away from them.﴾ ﴿And they used to carve houses out of the mountains, secure.﴾ ﴿So the Shriek seized them at morning.﴾ ﴿And what they used to earn did not avail them.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth. And indeed, the Hour is coming, so forgive with gracious forgiveness.﴾ ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Creator, the All-Knowing.﴾

"Al-Ayka" (al-ayka, the thicket): a dense, green cluster of trees, such as lote-trees and the like. Qatada said: It has been reported that the thicket of these people was of dum-palm trees. It was also said: of the muql tree, and it was said: of lote-trees. These people were a folk who dwelt in a thicket and benefited from it for their livelihoods. So God sent Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, to them, and they disbelieved. God then imposed heat upon them, and it lasted over them for seven days. Then they saw a cloud, so they went out and sheltered beneath it, and it blazed into fire over them.

al-Tabari related: Shu'ayb was sent to two nations that disbelieved, and they were punished with two different punishments. The people of Madyan were punished with the Shriek, and the companions of the Thicket were punished with the canopy (al-zulla). The readers did not differ in this place regarding the insertion of the alif and lam on "ayka." Most of them hamzated the alif of "ayka" after the lam. It was reported from some of them that he eased it and transferred its vowel to the lam, reading "al-ayka" without hamza. They differed regarding it in Surat al-Shu'ara' and in Surat Sad.

"Inna" here is the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy (thaqila), according to the school of the Basrans. Al-Farra' said: "in" means "ma" (not), and the lam in His saying "la-zalimin" means "illa" (except). Abu 'Ali said: "al-Ayk" is the plural of "ayka," like "tamra" and "tamr." Among the evidence for the word is the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

Like the weeping of doves over the branches
of the thicket, among the birds with lamenting cries.

(p. 313) And the verse of Jarir:

I stood there, and longing stirred in me,
while the doves of the thicket cooed to her in pairs.

And another's saying:

Behold, the world is but the freshness of a thicket:
when one side of it turns green, the other side dries up.

And the saying of al-Hudhali:

Adorned with two braids, close to her
is a cluster of the thicket, its short branches hanging over it.

And al-Asma'i recited:

And no deep-curved valley ... that casts onto the ground
the wood of the ayk and the dhall (tamarisk).

(p. 314) The pronoun in His saying "wa-innahuma" may refer to the two cities previously mentioned: the city of the people of Lot and the city of the companions of the Thicket. It may also refer to the two prophets, Lot and Shu'ayb, in that they are both upon a path from God and a clear law.

"Al-imam" in the speech of the Arabs is that which is followed and taken as a guide. They say it of the line used for building. It may be the road, it may be a clear book, it may be the measure by which craftsmen work, and it may be a man who is followed as an example, and the like. Whoever holds that the pronoun in "innahuma" returns to the two cities says: "al-imam" is the road. It was also said, on that basis: "al-imam" is the Book in which their destruction was predestined.

"Ashab al-Hijr" are Thamud, whose story has already been mentioned. "Al-Hijr" is their city, which lies between Medina and Tabuk. He said "al-mursalin" (the messengers) because whoever denies one messenger is required to deny all of them, since the matter of belief is one for all the messengers together. Thus this expression is more severe upon the deniers.

The signs that God gave them were the she-camel and what it contained of breaking the customary course, as its explanation and expansion were previously mentioned. Abu Haywa read "wa-atayna-hum ayatana" in the singular.

The majority of people read "yanhituna" with a kasra on the ha'. Al-Hasan read it with a fatha, and this is because of the throat letter (harf al-halq), and this is the reading of Abu Haywa. As for His saying "amin" (secure), it was said: its meaning is: safe from their collapse. It was said: safe from the calamities of this world. It was said: safe from death, due to their delusion through the length of their hopes.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak, and the most evident opinion regarding it is that they felt secure from the consequences of the Hereafter, (p. 315) so they did not act according to what it required, but rather acted according to the security they felt from it.

The meaning of "musbihin" is: upon their entering the morning. It is mentioned that this was a Saturday. The story of their punishment, their appointed time, and the changing of their colors has already been mentioned. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 15, verse 87–93:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the great Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to of them, [as] pairs, and do not grieve over them, and lower your wing to the believers.﴾ ﴿And say, "Indeed, I am the clear warner,"﴾ ﴿like what We sent down upon the dividers,﴾ ﴿[Those] who have made the Qur'an into parts.﴾ ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely ask them all﴾ ﴿about what they used to do.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr said: "The seven" here are the seven long [surahs]: al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, (p-316) al-A'raf, and al-Anfal together with Bara'ah. Ibn Jubayr said: rather, the seventh is Yunus, and al-Anfal and Bara'ah are not counted among them. According to these scholars, "al-mathani" (the oft-repeated) is the whole Qur'an, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿a Book consistent, oft-repeated﴾ [al-Zumar: 23]. It was called so because stories and reports are repeated and recurring within it.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas also, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Mulaykah, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and a group said: "The seven" here are the verses of praise (al-Hamd). Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are seven with the basmalah." Others said: "They are seven without the basmalah." A hadith on this has been narrated, the text of which is: "Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: 'Shall I not teach you, O Ubayy, a surah the like of which has not been sent down in the Torah, nor in the Gospel, nor in the Psalms, nor in the Furqan?' I said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Indeed I hope that you will not leave that door until you learn it.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up and I stood with him, my hand in his hand, and I began to slow down out of fear that he would leave. When I approached the door of the mosque I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the surah you promised me?' He said: 'How do you recite when you stand in prayer?' He said: So I recited ﴿Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2] until I finished the Opening of the Book. He said: 'It is it, and it is the seven oft-repeated and the great Qur'an which I have been given.'" Thus [or similar to this], it was mentioned by Malik in the Muwatta', and it is also narrated in al-Bukhari and Muslim from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla as well. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "It is the seven oft-repeated, the Mother of the Qur'an, and the Opening of the Book." In the book of al-Zahrawi: "and there is no basmalah in it." According to these scholars, "al-mathani" may be the Qur'an, so "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id). A group said: rather, it means the Opening (al-Hamd) itself, as He said: ﴿the impurity of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], so "min" is for specifying the kind (li-bayan al-jins). It was called so because it is repeated in every rak'ah. It was also said: it was called so because praise is offered through it to Allah, may He be exalted; al-Zajjaj permitted this, but there is a consideration from the standpoint of morphology (tasrif) regarding this view. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: it was called so (p-317) because Allah, may He be exalted, set it apart for this community and did not give it to anyone else. Ibn Abi Mulaykah said something similar. A group read "wal-Qur'ani" with a genitive (khafd) as a conjunction with "al-mathani," and a group read "wal-Qur'ana" with an accusative (nasb) as a conjunction with his saying "seven."

Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam said: What is meant by his saying "seven," i.e., seven meanings from the Qur'an, with which We granted you the honor of rank in this world and the Hereafter, and they are: command, forbid, give glad tidings, warn, strike parables, count the blessings, and expose the unseen.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: "The seven oft-repeated" is the verse of the Opening of the Book, and this surah was revealed before any of the long seven came down.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾, the verse. al-Tabari related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah that he said: This verse is a command to be content with the Book of Allah in place of all the adornment of this world, and it refers to his, peace and blessings be upon him, saying: "He is not of us who does not beautify his voice with the Qur'an" (i.e., who does not find sufficiency in it). It is as if He said: "We have given you something great and momentous, so do not look at anything else of the affairs of this world and its adornments with which We have given enjoyment to kinds of these disbelievers." From this same meaning is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever is given the Qur'an, then sees that someone has been given something better than what he has been given, has magnified the small and belittled the great." It is as if extending the eye is accompanied by longing (tamanni), and for this reason the inclination toward the adornment of this world was expressed by extending the eye. "Al-azwaj" here means kinds and likenesses.

His saying: ﴿and do not grieve over them﴾, i.e., do not be grieved at their disbelief and destruction; turn your face and your care toward those who believed in you, and lower for them your wing (p-318), and lower your sides to them. This is a metaphor meaning: soften your wing and humble your sides. "Al-janah" means the side and flank, and from it is His saying: ﴿and draw your hand to your side﴾ [Ta-Ha: 22]. So it is a command to incline toward them, and al-junuh means inclination.

﴿And say, "Indeed, I am the clear warner,"﴾, i.e., hold fast to this great portion which We have bestowed upon you. The kaf in his saying "kama" is connected to a verb omitted whose estimate is: "And say, 'Indeed, I am the warner of a punishment like that which We sent down upon the dividers.'" The kaf is a noun in the accusative position. This is the saying of the exegetes, but in my view it is not correct, because "kama" is not something Muhammad ﷺ says; rather it is from the saying of Allah, may He be exalted, to him, so the speech is separated. This saying is only consistent if we estimate that Allah, may He be exalted, said to him: "You warn of a punishment as..." What I say on this: the meaning is: "And say, 'I am a warner as Our messengers before you said, and We sent down to them as We sent down to you.'" It may also be that the meaning is: "And say, 'I am a warner, as We have stated in the Books that you will come as a warner,'" and this is on the basis that "al-muqtasimin" are the People of the Book.

People differed regarding "al-muqtasimin": who are they? Ibn Zayd said: they are the people of Salih who swore by Allah that they would surely attack him and his family by night, so "al-muqtasimun," on this view, derive from the oath (qasam).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is troubled by His saying: ﴿those who made the Qur'an into parts﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "al-muqtasimun" are the People of the Book who divided their religion, and made the Book of Allah into parts, believing in some and disbelieving in others. Mujahid said something similar.

A group said: "al-muqtasimun" are among the disbelievers of Quraysh who divided the paths at the time of the seasons to inform people about the condition of Muhammad ﷺ, and they made the Qur'an into sorcery, poetry and soothsaying, thus they "ʿadhahu" it (divided it) by this, and they "ʿaddhu" it into parts by this division.

'Ikrimah said: "al-muqtasimun" are a people who used to mock the surahs of the Qur'an, and one of them would say: "This surah is mine," and another would say: "And this one is mine."

His saying: "ʿidhin" is a second object, and "jaʿalu" means "ṣayyaru" (made), i.e., with their tongues and claims. The most apparent thing about it is that it is the plural of ʿidhah, which is a portion of a thing, and a group of people, like thubah and thubin, and ʿizah and ʿizin. Its original form is ʿidhahah and thawbah, so the ya and nun are a substitute for the deleted element, just as they said sanah and sunun, since its original is sanhah. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "ʿidhin" is derived from al-ʿadha' (the limbs), i.e., they tore it apart and made it sections and limbs, and from this is the saying of the rajiz:

Allah's religion is not something divided into parts.

This is the choice of Abu 'Ubaydah. Qatadah said: "ʿidhin" is derived from al-ʿadah, which is obscene slander, so Quraysh slandered the Book of Allah by their saying: it is poetry, it is sorcery, it is soothsaying. This is the choice of al-Kisa'i. A group said: "ʿidhin" is the plural of ʿidhah, which is a name for sorcery specifically in the dialect of Quraysh, and from it is the saying of the rajiz:

For the water, from their ʿidhat, is Zamzamah.

'Ikrimah, the freedman of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said this and said: al-ʿadhah is sorcery, and they call the female sorceress "al-ʿadhihah." In a hadith: "Allah has cursed the ʿadhihah and the mustaʿdhihah" (p-320), and this is the choice of al-Farra'.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Whoever said "they made it limbs" meant: they divided it as a slaughtered camel is divided into limbs.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely ask them all﴾ to the end of the verse: it is a general pronoun and a pure threat, taking each person to account according to his crime and disobedience. The disbeliever is asked about "there is no god but Allah," and about the messengers, and about his disbelief and intention; the sinful believer is asked about his neglect; the imam about his subjects; and every accountable person about what he was charged to carry out. There are hadiths on this.

Abu al-'Aliyah said in explanation of this verse: all the servants will be asked on the Day of Resurrection about two things: what they used to worship, and what they answered the messengers. Anas ibn Malik, Ibn 'Umar, and Mujahid said in its explanation: the question is about "there is no god but Allah," and al-Zahrawi mentioned it from the Prophet ﷺ.

Ibn 'Abbas said regarding his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely ask them all﴾ ﴿about what they used to do﴾: it will be said to them: "Why did you do such-and-such?" He said: And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So on that Day no human or jinn will be asked about his sin﴾ [al-Rahman: 39] means: it will not be said to him, "What did you sin?" because Allah, may He be exalted, knows about his sin better than he does. Negating the question is negating the pure interrogation, while affirming the question is by way of establishing the proof against them and rebuking them.
